questions.title: Writing a Query to Find Duplicate Supplier Invoices
questions.prompt: Write a SQL query against AP_INVOICES(invoice_id, supplier_id, invoice_number, invoice_amount, invoice_date) that identifies potential duplicate invoices — the same supplier, same invoice number, submitted more than once — and returns the supplier, invoice number, count, and total amount at risk.
questions.code:
SELECT
    supplier_id,
    invoice_number,
    COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count,
    SUM(invoice_amount) AS total_amount_at_risk
FROM ap_invoices
GROUP BY supplier_id, invoice_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY total_amount_at_risk DESC;
questions.modelAnswer:
The query groups invoices by the combination of supplier_id and invoice_number, because a duplicate invoice is defined relative to a specific supplier — the same invoice_number from two different suppliers is coincidence, not a duplicate. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filters the grouped result to only combinations that appear more than once, which is the correct place for this filter since it operates on an aggregate (COUNT), not a raw column — WHERE could not express this condition.

SUM(invoice_amount) in each group gives the total dollar exposure at risk for that duplicate pair, and ordering descending surfaces the highest-value potential duplicates first, which is what an AP manager reviewing this list would want prioritized.

A stronger answer would flag a real-world refinement: exact invoice_number string matching can miss duplicates with trivial formatting differences (leading zeros, different case, extra whitespace), so a production version of this check might normalize invoice_number (TRIM, UPPER, strip leading zeros) before grouping, and would also want to join to a status column to exclude invoices already identified and cancelled as known duplicates, which would otherwise keep reappearing in this report.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd group by supplier and invoice number together, not invoice number alone — because invoice number by itself isn't meaningful across suppliers, two different suppliers can easily use '1001' as an invoice number and that's not a duplicate, that's just coincidence. Then I use HAVING, not WHERE, to filter down to groups that show up more than once, because that condition is checking a COUNT, which is an aggregate — WHERE runs before grouping happens, so it can't see that.

I'd sum the invoice amount per group too, so this isn't just a list of suspicious pairs, it's a dollar-prioritized list — whoever's reviewing this wants to look at the biggest exposure first, not alphabetically. The thing I'd flag as a real caveat, though: this only catches exact string matches on invoice number. If one invoice number has a leading zero and the duplicate doesn't, or there's trailing whitespace from a data entry error, this query misses it entirely. For a real production check I'd normalize the invoice number — trim it, upper-case it, maybe strip leading zeros — before grouping, and I'd also want to exclude invoices already flagged and cancelled as known duplicates so they don't keep showing up on this report every time someone runs it.
questions.example: Supplier 4021, invoice number 'INV-5590' appears twice with amounts $3,200 and $3,200 → duplicate_count = 2, total_amount_at_risk = $6,400, surfaced near the top of the descending-sorted list.
commonMistakes: Grouping by invoice_number alone instead of supplier_id + invoice_number
Using WHERE instead of HAVING to filter on the aggregate COUNT
Not summing or otherwise quantifying the dollar exposure, just listing duplicate pairs
Assuming exact string match is sufficient without acknowledging formatting-variant duplicates
Not considering that previously-identified and cancelled duplicates would reappear in the result
keyPoints: Correctly groups by supplier_id and invoice_number together
Correctly uses HAVING (not WHERE) to filter on an aggregate condition
Computes and sorts by dollar exposure, not just occurrence count
Acknowledges the limits of exact string matching for real-world duplicate detection
Considers excluding already-resolved/cancelled duplicates from future runs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GROUP BY grain (supplier + invoice number)
Correct use of HAVING vs. WHERE for the aggregate filter
Computes and prioritizes by dollar exposure
Identifies real-world limitations of exact-match duplicate detection

questions.title: Building AR Aging Buckets with CASE
questions.prompt: Write a SQL query against AR_TRANSACTIONS(transaction_id, customer_id, amount_due, due_date) that classifies each open receivable into aging buckets — Current, 1-30 Days Past Due, 31-60 Days Past Due, 61-90 Days Past Due, and Over 90 Days — relative to SYSDATE, and summarizes total amount due per bucket.
questions.code:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN SYSDATE <= due_date THEN 'Current'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 1 AND 30 THEN '1-30 Days Past Due'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 31 AND 60 THEN '31-60 Days Past Due'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 61 AND 90 THEN '61-90 Days Past Due'
        ELSE 'Over 90 Days'
    END AS aging_bucket,
    SUM(amount_due) AS total_amount_due
FROM ar_transactions
WHERE amount_due > 0
GROUP BY
    CASE
        WHEN SYSDATE <= due_date THEN 'Current'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 1 AND 30 THEN '1-30 Days Past Due'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 31 AND 60 THEN '31-60 Days Past Due'
        WHEN SYSDATE - due_date BETWEEN 61 AND 90 THEN '61-90 Days Past Due'
        ELSE 'Over 90 Days'
    END
ORDER BY MIN(SYSDATE - due_date);
questions.modelAnswer:
The query uses a CASE expression to classify each transaction row based on how many days past its due_date the current date (SYSDATE) is, with explicit, non-overlapping boundary conditions (1-30, 31-60, 61-90, and a catch-all ELSE for anything beyond 90) so every row lands in exactly one bucket with no gaps or double-counting at the boundaries. The WHERE amount_due > 0 filter excludes fully paid or zero-balance transactions, since an aging report should only reflect open, unpaid exposure.

Because the bucket label is a computed expression rather than a stored column, the GROUP BY must repeat the full CASE expression (Oracle SQL does not allow grouping by a SELECT-list alias directly in the same way some other databases do), and the same repeated expression is the cleanest way to ensure the grouping matches the display labeling exactly.

The ORDER BY uses MIN(SYSDATE - due_date) per group rather than ordering alphabetically by the bucket label, which would incorrectly sort '1-30 Days Past Due' before 'Current' or '31-60' depending on string sort order — ordering by the underlying day count ensures the buckets display in their natural aging progression (Current, then increasingly overdue).
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build the bucket as a CASE expression off SYSDATE minus due_date, and the thing I'd be careful about is making sure the boundaries don't overlap or leave gaps — 1 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90, then an ELSE that catches everything past 90, so every row falls into exactly one bucket, nothing falls through the cracks and nothing double-counts at a boundary like day 30 versus day 31. I'd also filter out anything with zero or negative amount_due up front, since an aging report shouldn't include stuff that's already fully paid.

One detail that trips people up in Oracle specifically: you can't group by a column alias the way you might expect, so I have to repeat the whole CASE expression in the GROUP BY, not just the label. And for the ORDER BY, I wouldn't sort by the bucket label alphabetically, because 'Current' and '1-30 Days Past Due' would sort in a weird order that doesn't match how anyone actually wants to read an aging report — I'd order by the minimum day count in each bucket instead, so it reads top to bottom as Current, then more and more overdue, the way people actually expect an aging schedule to look.
questions.example: A transaction with due_date 45 days ago falls into '31-60 Days Past Due'; a transaction due_date 5 days in the future falls into 'Current'; both are summed into their respective bucket totals.
commonMistakes: Leaving gaps or overlaps at bucket boundaries (e.g., both a '1-30' and '30-60' bucket double-counting day 30)
Forgetting to exclude zero/negative amount_due rows from the aging report
Attempting to GROUP BY a SELECT-list alias instead of repeating the full CASE expression
Sorting the final result alphabetically by bucket label instead of by underlying aging order
Not handling transactions not yet due (future due_date) with an explicit 'Current' case
keyPoints: Builds non-overlapping, gap-free CASE boundaries for each aging bucket
Correctly filters to open/unpaid balances before aggregating
Correctly repeats the CASE expression in GROUP BY per Oracle SQL rules
Orders results by underlying aging progression, not alphabetically
Handles the 'Current' (not yet due) case explicitly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: CASE expression boundaries are correct, non-overlapping, and gap-free
Correctly filters and aggregates open balances per bucket
Correctly handles GROUP BY on a computed expression in Oracle SQL
Orders results in natural aging progression rather than alphabetically

questions.title: Finding Purchase Orders with No Matching Receipt Using NOT EXISTS
questions.prompt: Write a SQL query against PO_HEADERS(po_id, supplier_id, po_date, po_status) and RECEIPTS(receipt_id, po_id, receipt_date, received_quantity) that finds every approved purchase order (po_status = 'Approved') older than 30 days that has no matching receipt record at all — a sign that goods were never received or receiving wasn't entered.
questions.code:
SELECT
    po.po_id,
    po.supplier_id,
    po.po_date
FROM po_headers po
WHERE po.po_status = 'Approved'
  AND po.po_date < SYSDATE - 30
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM receipts r
      WHERE r.po_id = po.po_id
  )
ORDER BY po.po_date;
questions.modelAnswer:
The query uses a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery rather than a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check, both of which are valid approaches, but NOT EXISTS communicates intent cleanly ('no row in RECEIPTS exists for this PO') and avoids the common pitfall of a LEFT JOIN approach, which is forgetting to filter specifically on the joined table's key being NULL (r.receipt_id IS NULL) rather than accidentally filtering on a column that could legitimately be NULL for other reasons.

The outer WHERE clause narrows to po_status = 'Approved' (excluding draft, cancelled, or closed POs, which wouldn't be meaningful exceptions) and po_date older than 30 days, which is a reasonable business rule for 'this should have been received by now' rather than flagging every recently-issued PO that simply hasn't had time to be received yet.

A complete answer would note the subquery is correlated — it references po.po_id from the outer query — which is what makes NOT EXISTS evaluate per-PO rather than as a single static check, and would also flag that this only detects POs with zero receipts; a PO that's partially received (some lines received, others not) requires a different, line-level comparison that this query does not address.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd use NOT EXISTS here rather than a LEFT JOIN with an IS NULL filter, mostly because it says exactly what I mean — 'give me POs where no row in receipts exists for this PO' — and it sidesteps a classic LEFT JOIN mistake where someone filters on the wrong column being NULL and gets a subtly wrong result. The subquery is correlated to the outer PO, so it's actually checking per-PO, not running once for the whole table.

On the filter side, I'd only look at approved POs — no point flagging a draft or a cancelled PO as a 'missing receipt' exception, that's just noise — and I'd only flag ones older than 30 days, because a PO issued yesterday hasn't had receiving fall behind yet, it just hasn't had time. The one thing I'd be upfront about: this only catches POs with zero receipts at all. If a PO has three lines and two got received but one didn't, this query won't catch that — that's a different, line-level check, and I'd want to build that as a follow-up if the business needs it.
questions.example: PO 8821, approved 45 days ago, has no rows in RECEIPTS → appears in the result as an exception. PO 8822, approved 45 days ago, has one receipt row → correctly excluded, even if that PO has unreceived lines the query doesn't check.
commonMistakes: Using a LEFT JOIN but filtering on the wrong column, producing an incorrect NULL check
Forgetting to correlate the subquery to the outer query's po_id
Not filtering po_status, flagging draft or cancelled POs as false exceptions
Applying no age threshold, flagging recently-issued POs that simply haven't had time to be received
Claiming this query also catches partially-received POs, which it does not
keyPoints: Correctly uses a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery
Correctly filters to relevant PO status and a meaningful age threshold
Explains why NOT EXISTS avoids a common LEFT JOIN/NULL-check pitfall
Acknowledges the query only detects zero-receipt POs, not partial receipt gaps
Orders or presents results in a business-usable way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, correlated NOT EXISTS subquery logic
Appropriate status and age filtering on the outer query
Explains the NOT EXISTS vs. LEFT JOIN/NULL tradeoff accurately
Correctly scopes the limitation (zero-receipt only, not partial)

lessonLink.label: Finding Missing Records with NOT EXISTS

questions.title: Populating an FBDI Supplier Import Template Correctly
questions.prompt: You're loading 200 new suppliers into Oracle Fusion using the Suppliers FBDI template. Walk through, specifically, how you'd approach filling in the template correctly for a bulk load — what you'd check before touching a single row, and the two or three mistakes on this specific template that most often cause a clean-looking file to fail at import.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts before any data entry: opening the template's instructions/field-reference tab to identify which columns are required versus optional for the Suppliers object specifically, which fields have a fixed list of valid values (e.g., supplier type, payment terms code, which must match an exact value already configured in the target environment, not a free-text description), and which fields expect a specific format (dates, lookup codes) rather than free text.

The answer should name specific, template-typical failure patterns: (1) payment terms or supplier type values that don't exactly match a value already set up in the environment (a typo or a value that exists in a different environment but not this one) — these pass template validation but fail at import with a 'value not found' style error; (2) duplicate or malformed Tax Identification Numbers / TINs that trip business validation rules around supplier uniqueness; (3) leaving a required site or address sub-structure incomplete, since suppliers in Oracle Fusion typically require at least one valid site, and a supplier header with no valid site can fail or create an unusable supplier record; (4) copy-paste from a source system that carries over hidden formatting (text that looks like a number but is actually formatted as text, extra whitespace) that causes a data-type mismatch during import even though the cell looks correct.

A complete answer describes validating a small batch (5-10 suppliers) end-to-end before committing to the full 200-row load, specifically to catch configuration-value mismatches early rather than discovering them after generating and uploading the full file.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I type anything into the template, I'd read the field reference tab first — every FBDI template has one — to know exactly which columns are required, which ones have a fixed list of valid values, and which ones expect a specific format. That's non-negotiable for me, because guessing at that stuff is exactly how you end up with a file that looks complete but fails at import.

On this specific template, there are a few mistakes I see constantly. First, payment terms codes and supplier type values have to match something already configured in that exact environment — not just 'a reasonable value,' the exact code, and a typo or a value that exists in a different instance will pass the template's own checks but blow up at import with a value-not-found error. Second, duplicate or malformed tax ID numbers — suppliers often have uniqueness rules around TINs that reject the row. Third, incomplete site or address data — a supplier generally needs at least one valid site, and if that sub-structure is missing or wrong, you can end up with a supplier record that technically imports but isn't usable for transactions. And a sneaky one: if this data came from a copy-paste out of another system, numbers sometimes get carried over as text with invisible formatting, and that silently breaks a field that looks totally fine to your eyes.

Given all that, I would never run all 200 rows first. I'd load five or ten as a test batch, run them through the full process, and fix anything that breaks there before committing to the full file — it's much cheaper to catch a payment-terms typo in a 5-row test than to chase it down across 200 rows of rejected interface data.
questions.example: A supplier row has Payment Terms = 'Net 30 Days' entered as free text, but the environment's configured value is exactly 'Net 30' — the template accepts the text, but the import process rejects the row because the value doesn't match any configured payment terms code.
commonMistakes: Entering free-text values for fields that require an exact match to a pre-configured list (payment terms, supplier type)
Not validating TIN/tax ID uniqueness and format before the bulk load
Leaving site/address sub-structure incomplete, producing an unusable supplier record
Not checking for hidden formatting from copy-pasted source data (numbers stored as text)
Loading the full 200-row file without first validating a small test batch
keyPoints: Reviews the template's field reference/instructions before entering data
Identifies specific Suppliers-template failure patterns (payment terms/type mismatches, TIN issues, incomplete sites, hidden formatting)
Explains why these specific issues pass template-level checks but fail at import
Recommends validating a small test batch before the full load
Demonstrates practical, specific knowledge rather than generic FBDI advice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sound pre-data-entry review process (field reference, required/valid values)
Names specific, accurate Suppliers-template failure patterns
Explains why these issues pass template checks but fail at import
Recommends a test-batch validation approach before full load

questions.title: Generating and Verifying the CSV/ZIP Output from an FBDI Template
questions.prompt: You've finished populating an FBDI template for GL journal import. Walk through exactly what happens when you click 'Generate CSV File,' what you should verify about the resulting file before uploading it, and one specific way this step silently produces a bad file even when the generation itself reports success.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer describes the macro-driven generation step: clicking 'Generate CSV File' runs embedded macro logic that reads every populated data row, validates basic structural rules the macro itself checks (such as required columns not being blank, in some templates), writes the data into one or more CSV files matching the exact column order and naming convention Oracle's import process expects, and packages them into a ZIP archive with the specific file-naming pattern required for upload — this is a mechanical, template-driven step, not a business-rule validation step.

Before uploading, the answer should describe opening the generated CSV (in a plain text viewer, not Excel, to avoid Excel re-formatting values on open) to spot-check that numeric and date values rendered as expected, that no column shifted due to a hidden/inserted row or column in the source template, and that the row count in the CSV matches the expected row count from the source data — a mismatch here means something in the template (a blank row, a merged cell, a hidden row) broke the generation silently.

The specific silent-failure scenario the answer should name: a date or amount formatted as text in Excel (common after a paste from another system) generates into the CSV looking correct to the eye but may be interpreted differently by the import process than a native numeric/date cell would be, or an extra blank row in the middle of the data range gets included as an empty row in the CSV, which generation reports as 'successful' because structurally nothing is wrong — the failure only surfaces later, at the import validation step, as a rejected or malformed row.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Clicking Generate CSV File runs a macro that's baked into the template — it reads every row you've filled in, checks whatever basic structural rules that specific template enforces, and writes it all out into CSV files in the exact column order and naming pattern Oracle's import expects, then zips it up correctly. It's a mechanical step, not a business-rule check — it's not confirming your account combinations are valid, just that the file is structured the way the import process wants to receive it.

Before I upload anything, I open the generated CSV in a plain text editor, not Excel, because Excel will happily reformat values the second it opens the file, which defeats the point of checking what's actually in it. I'm looking for the row count matching what I expect from my source data, and for dates and amounts rendering the way I expect, not shifted into the wrong column because of a hidden row or a merged cell upstream in the template.

The specific silent trap I'd call out: if a value got pasted in as text instead of a real number or date — which happens all the time when people copy out of another system — the CSV will generate 'successfully' and look completely fine to your eye, but the import process can interpret that value differently than it would a proper numeric or date cell. Generation reports success because structurally the file is fine — the actual problem doesn't show up until the import step rejects or mangles that row, and by then it's a confusing error instead of an obvious one.
questions.example: A journal amount pasted in as text ('1250.00' left-aligned, formatted as text) generates into the CSV without error, but the import process's numeric parsing handles it differently than a true numeric cell, leading to a rejected or misread row discovered only at the import validation stage.
commonMistakes: Opening the generated CSV in Excel to verify it, which re-formats values and hides the actual problem
Assuming 'Generate CSV File reported success' means the data itself is valid
Not comparing the generated row count against the expected source row count
Not recognizing text-formatted numbers/dates as a silent risk that passes generation but fails or misbehaves at import
Treating generation as a business-rule validation step rather than a mechanical formatting step
keyPoints: Correctly describes generation as a mechanical, template-driven step, not business validation
Describes verifying the CSV in a plain text viewer, not Excel
Checks row count and column alignment against expected source data
Names text-formatted numeric/date values as a specific silent-failure risk
Distinguishes generation-time success from import-time validation success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately describes what the generation step actually does and does not validate
Describes a sound pre-upload verification process
Correctly identifies the text-formatted value silent-failure scenario
Distinguishes generation-time success from import-time validation

questions.title: Walking Through an End-to-End Payables Invoice FBDI Load
questions.prompt: A client wants to migrate 3,000 open AP invoices from their legacy system into Oracle Fusion using FBDI, instead of entering them manually. Walk through the end-to-end steps you'd actually perform, from source data extract to the invoices being usable in Payables.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer walks through the full sequence: (1) extracting and mapping the legacy invoice data to the Payables Invoices FBDI template's required columns, including resolving legacy supplier identifiers to the already-migrated Oracle Fusion supplier IDs/numbers — a load cannot succeed if supplier references don't resolve; (2) populating the template, including header-level invoice data and the associated distribution lines (account, amount, line type), since invoices require at least one valid distribution; (3) generating the CSV/ZIP via the template macro and spot-checking a sample before upload; (4) uploading to UCM and running Load Interface File for Import to move rows into the Payables open interface tables; (5) running the Import Payables Invoices scheduled process, which validates each row (valid supplier/site, valid distribution accounts, required fields) and creates real invoice records for valid rows while rejecting invalid ones with specific errors; (6) reviewing the import results report, correcting and resubmitting any rejected rows; (7) spot-checking a sample of successfully created invoices directly in the Payables work area to confirm they display and behave correctly (correct amounts, correct supplier, correct distributions) before considering the migration complete.

The answer should flag migration-specific considerations beyond a routine load: whether these invoices need to carry their original legacy invoice numbers for audit traceability, whether they should bypass normal matching/approval workflows since they represent already-approved historical balances, and whether accounting needs to be created for them or whether opening balances are being handled separately — these are implementation decisions that affect how the template is populated, not just technical FBDI mechanics.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this as two problems: the data problem and the FBDI mechanics. On the data side, the first real risk is supplier references — every one of these 3,000 invoices needs to resolve to a supplier that already exists in Fusion, so if supplier migration isn't fully done and verified first, this load is dead on arrival. I'd also want to know upfront whether these need to preserve the original legacy invoice number for audit purposes, and whether they should skip normal approval workflows, since these aren't new invoices coming in, they're historical balances being converted.

Mechanically: populate the Payables Invoices FBDI template, header data plus at least one distribution line per invoice since Payables won't accept an invoice with no distribution. Generate the CSV, spot check it in a text editor, upload to UCM, run Load Interface File for Import to get rows into the open interface tables, then run Import Payables Invoices. That process validates every row — supplier, site, account combination, required fields — and creates real invoices for anything valid while rejecting the rest with specific errors I can act on.

After that I don't just call it done — I pull the import results report, fix and resubmit whatever got rejected, and then I go spot-check a sample of the successfully created invoices directly in the Payables work area, not just trust the import log, because I want to see with my own eyes that the amounts, supplier, and distributions actually look right before I tell the client this migration is finished.
questions.example: 3,000 legacy invoices map to the FBDI template; 2,964 import cleanly on the first pass; 36 reject because their legacy supplier code didn't resolve to a migrated Oracle Fusion supplier number — corrected by fixing the supplier cross-reference and resubmitting just those 36 rows.
commonMistakes: Not verifying legacy supplier references resolve to migrated Oracle Fusion supplier records before building the file
Populating invoice headers without the required distribution line(s)
Treating the migration as purely a technical FBDI exercise without raising implementation decisions (invoice numbering, approval bypass, opening balance accounting)
Considering the load complete once the import process reports success, without spot-checking actual invoice records
Resubmitting the entire file after a partial rejection instead of correcting and resubmitting only the rejected rows
keyPoints: Correctly sequences the full pipeline: data mapping → template population → generation → upload → interface load → import → validation/correction
Identifies supplier reference resolution as a migration-specific prerequisite risk
Includes distribution-line population as a required part of invoice header data
Raises migration-specific implementation questions beyond pure FBDI mechanics
Describes verifying actual invoice records post-import, not just trusting the import log

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly and completely sequences the end-to-end migration pipeline
Identifies supplier reference resolution as a critical migration prerequisite
Raises relevant migration-specific implementation questions
Describes sound post-import validation beyond trusting the import log

questions.title: Constructing a REST GET Request to Filter and Page Through Invoices
questions.prompt: Write the REST API call (URL with query parameters) you'd use against Oracle Fusion's invoices resource to retrieve only invoices for a specific supplier, with an invoice date on or after 2026-01-01, returning results 26-50 of the match (i.e., the second page of a 25-per-page result set), sorted by invoice date descending.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query parameter q carries the filter expression, using the finder/query syntax Oracle Fusion REST resources expect: multiple conditions joined with a semicolon act as an implicit AND, so SupplierId=12345;InvoiceDate>=2026-01-01 returns only rows matching both conditions. orderBy specifies the sort field and direction (InvoiceDate:desc for descending), which must be applied before paging parameters are meaningful, since 'the second page' is only a stable concept relative to a defined sort order.

For paging, limit sets the page size (25) and offset sets how many matching rows to skip before starting the returned page — to get results 26-50, offset must be 25 (skip the first 25), not 26 or 50, which is the most common off-by-one mistake with offset-based paging. The answer should note that limit and offset operate on the already-filtered and already-sorted result set, not on the full unfiltered table, so changing the filter or sort without adjusting expectations about what 'page 2' contains is a common source of confusing bugs.

A complete answer would also flag that offset-based paging can produce inconsistent results if records are being inserted or deleted between page requests (a row shifting position between calls to page 1 and page 2), and that some APIs offer a more stable cursor-based alternative, which is worth knowing even if offset/limit is what's being used here.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build the filter using the q parameter with the semicolon syntax Oracle's REST resources use for combining conditions — SupplierId equals the target, and invoice date is greater than or equal to January 1st, 2026, joined with a semicolon so both conditions apply together. Then orderBy for the sort, InvoiceDate colon desc for descending, and that has to come before I even think about paging, because 'page two' only makes sense relative to a specific, stable sort order.

For paging, limit is the page size, twenty-five, and offset is how many rows to skip before the page starts. The thing people get wrong constantly is the math on offset — if you want results 26 through 50, offset is 25, not 26, because it's 'skip this many,' not 'start at this row number.' I'd also mention, since it's relevant here even if not asked directly, that offset-based paging can get weird if rows are being inserted or deleted between your page-1 and page-2 calls — a row can shift position and you either see a duplicate or miss one. It's not usually a dealbreaker, but it's worth knowing before you build something that depends on paging being perfectly stable.
questions.example: GET /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/invoices?q=SupplierId=12345;InvoiceDate>=2026-01-01&orderBy=InvoiceDate:desc&limit=25&offset=25 — returns the 26th through 50th matching invoices for supplier 12345 dated on or after Jan 1, 2026, newest first.
commonMistakes: Using offset=26 or offset=50 instead of the correct offset=25 to get results 26-50
Omitting orderBy, making 'page 2' an unstable/undefined concept
Joining multiple filter conditions with the wrong syntax instead of the expected semicolon-delimited AND
Not recognizing that limit/offset apply to the filtered and sorted set, not the raw table
Failing to mention the stability risk of offset-based paging under concurrent inserts/deletes
keyPoints: Correctly constructs the filter expression with the proper query syntax
Correctly applies orderBy before paging for a stable result ordering
Correctly calculates offset for the requested result range
Explains limit/offset as operating on the filtered, sorted set
Notes the stability limitation of offset-based paging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct filter syntax for supplier and date conditions
Correct orderBy usage and placement relative to paging
Correct offset/limit calculation for the requested result range
Explains the limitation/risk of offset-based paging

questions.title: Constructing a REST POST Payload to Create a Supplier Invoice
questions.prompt: Write the JSON body you'd send in a POST request to Oracle Fusion's invoices REST resource to create a new AP invoice for supplier ID 20456, invoice number 'INV-9981', invoice date 2026-10-01, invoice amount $4,500.00, with a single distribution line for $4,500.00 charged to account combination '01-000-7420-0000-000'.
questions.modelAnswer:
The JSON structures the invoice header fields (SupplierId, InvoiceNumber, InvoiceDate, InvoiceAmount, and a currency, which is required even if defaulted elsewhere in the UI) as top-level attributes, and nests the distribution/line information inside a child array (invoiceLines) rather than as flat sibling fields — this mirrors how Oracle Fusion's invoice resource models a one-to-many relationship between an invoice header and its lines, and is a common place integration developers get it wrong by trying to flatten a nested resource into a single flat object.

The answer should note that the header-level InvoiceAmount and the sum of line-level Amount values must agree (here, both $4,500.00) — a mismatch between header total and summed line amounts is a validation failure independent of anything else being correct, since the invoice must balance internally before Payables will accept it. Date format should follow the ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) convention the API expects rather than a locale-specific format.

A complete answer would flag that field names must exactly match the resource's documented schema (case-sensitive, exact attribute names) — a plausible-looking field name that doesn't match the schema causes the request to fail or the field to be silently ignored depending on the API's behavior, and that this payload intentionally omits optional fields not specified in the prompt (e.g., payment terms, description) rather than guessing at values not given.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd put the header-level stuff — supplier, invoice number, date, total amount, and currency, since that's required even though people forget it — as top-level fields, and then nest the distribution line inside an invoiceLines array, because that's a child collection, not a flat sibling field. That's the part people get wrong most often when they're new to this — they try to flatten everything into one object instead of respecting the one-to-many structure the resource actually has.

The detail I'd double check before sending this: the header InvoiceAmount and the sum of all the line amounts have to match exactly — here it's simple because there's only one line for the full $4,500, but on a multi-line invoice that's a real validation point, the invoice has to balance internally or it gets rejected regardless of anything else being correct. I'd also make sure the date's in ISO format, year-month-day, not something locale-specific like month-day-year, since that's what the API expects. And field names have to match the documented schema exactly — case and spelling both — a close-but-not-exact field name either errors out or just gets silently dropped, which is worse because then you think it worked and it didn't actually set that value.
questions.example: A header InvoiceAmount of 4500.00 with two distribution lines summing to 4000.00 and 400.00 (total 4400.00) would fail validation — the header and line totals must reconcile exactly before the invoice is accepted.
commonMistakes: Flattening the distribution line into top-level fields instead of a nested invoiceLines array
Letting header InvoiceAmount and summed line amounts disagree
Using a locale-specific date format instead of ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD)
Using a plausible but incorrect field name that doesn't match the documented schema exactly
Omitting the required currency field
keyPoints: Correctly structures header fields as top-level attributes and lines as a nested child array
Ensures header InvoiceAmount reconciles with the sum of line amounts
Uses correct ISO date formatting
Uses exact, schema-matching field names
Includes required fields (currency) without inventing unspecified optional values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct nested structure for header vs. line-level data
Header and line amount reconciliation is correct and explained
Correct date formatting and required field inclusion
Explains the risk of inexact field names against the documented schema

questions.title: Configuring Accounting Distributions on a Requisition
questions.prompt: A requisition for a $12,000 software subscription needs to be split across two cost centers (70% Marketing, 30% IT) instead of the single default distribution the requester's default expense account would normally produce. Walk through how you'd configure the accounting distributions on this requisition line to achieve that split correctly.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that the requisition line's distribution defaults from the requester's assigned expense account (typically driven by their default expense account setup or project/task context), but that default can be overridden at the line level by splitting the single distribution into multiple distribution rows, each with its own account and either a percentage or an amount. The candidate should describe navigating to the distributions section of the requisition line, changing from a single distribution to multiple, and entering two rows: one at 70% (or $8,400) coded to the Marketing cost center segment of the account combination, and one at 30% (or $3,600) coded to IT's cost center segment, keeping all other segments (company, natural account) consistent with what the single-line default would have used unless those also need to differ.

The answer should note that the system should validate that the split percentages sum to 100% (or amounts sum to the full line amount) before the requisition can be submitted, and that this distribution split carries forward through the transaction — when the requisition is processed into a purchase order and later matched to an invoice, the distributions (and their split) typically flow through rather than needing to be re-entered at every stage, which is why getting the split right at the requisition stage matters for downstream accuracy.

A complete answer would mention validating the resulting account combinations against the chart of accounts (confirming '...Marketing cost center...' and '...IT cost center...' are both valid, active combinations) before submitting, since an invalid combination would block approval or accounting later in the chain.
questions.professionalAnswer:
By default, that requisition line is going to pick up one distribution based on the requester's default expense account — one account, one hundred percent. To split it, I'd go into the distributions section on the line and switch it from a single distribution to multiple, then add two rows: one at 70%, coded with the Marketing cost center segment, and one at 30%, coded with IT's cost center segment, keeping everything else — company, natural account — the same as what the default would've used, unless those actually need to change too.

The system should stop me if those percentages don't add up to 100, which is a good sanity check before I submit. And I'd want to flag why getting this right at the requisition stage actually matters beyond just this document — that distribution split generally carries forward when the requisition becomes a PO and eventually gets matched to an invoice, so if I get the split wrong here, I'm not just fixing one document later, I'm potentially chasing it through the PO and the invoice too. Before I submit, I'd also double check both of those full account combinations are actually valid and active in the chart of accounts — an invalid combination on either split line is going to block this at approval or cause a mess downstream.
questions.example: Requisition line, $12,000: Distribution 1 — 70% ($8,400), cost center = Marketing; Distribution 2 — 30% ($3,600), cost center = IT. Both validated as active account combinations before submission.

Entering percentages that don't sum to 100% or amounts that don't sum to the full line amount
Changing unrelated account segments (natural account, company) that should have stayed consistent with the default
Not validating that both resulting account combinations are valid and active
Assuming the split needs to be manually re-entered at the PO and invoice stage rather than flowing forward

Correctly applies the 70/30 split by percentage or amount on the correct segment

questions.title: Configuring AutoInvoice Grouping Rules for a Multi-Line Sales Order
questions.prompt: A customer wants every sales order shipped to them in a single calendar week to be billed on one consolidated invoice, rather than receiving a separate invoice per shipment. Explain what you'd configure in the AutoInvoice grouping setup to achieve this, and what would prevent two lines from grouping even if this rule is set up correctly.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that AutoInvoice grouping is controlled by grouping rule attributes — the set of transaction fields that must match for multiple fulfillment lines to be combined onto a single invoice. To consolidate by customer and calendar week, the grouping rule would need to include the customer (bill-to) and a date attribute bucketed to the week rather than the exact ship date, since grouping by exact date would still split shipments on different days within the same week onto separate invoices — Oracle Fusion grouping is typically configured around specific attribute matches rather than an automatic 'any date in the same week' concept, so achieving this often requires a custom grouping rule or transaction source configuration that normalizes the date attribute used for grouping to a week-level value.

The answer should explain what prevents grouping even when the rule is configured correctly: any mismatch on an attribute included in the grouping rule — different bill-to site, different currency, different payment terms, different transaction type — will force lines onto separate invoices regardless of the week-based intent, because grouping requires an exact match on every attribute the rule considers, not just the ones the business cares about. This is a frequent real-world gap between what a client assumes grouping should do ('it's the same customer, why are these two invoices?') and what it actually checks.

A complete answer notes that this should be tested with representative data covering the edge cases (a shipment on the week boundary, a shipment with different payment terms than the rest) before being presented to the client as solved.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Grouping rules work by matching specific attributes across fulfillment lines — if every attribute the rule checks matches, the lines combine onto one invoice. To get a week-level consolidation, I'd need the rule to key off the customer and a week-level date value, not the exact ship date, because if I group on exact date, two shipments three days apart in the same week still end up on separate invoices — that's not what the client's asking for. Getting true 'same calendar week' grouping usually isn't a default out-of-the-box behavior, so this often means normalizing the date attribute being used for grouping, or building that logic into the transaction source configuration, rather than assuming the standard setup does it automatically.

The part I'd make sure the client understands upfront: even with that rule configured correctly, anything else the rule also checks has to match too — bill-to site, currency, payment terms, transaction type. If one shipment that week has different payment terms than the others, for whatever reason, it's going to split onto its own invoice regardless of being the same customer and same week — and that's usually the moment a client calls and says 'why didn't these group,' not because the rule is broken, but because they didn't realize every attribute in the rule has to match, not just the ones they personally care about. I'd test this with a few deliberately awkward cases — a shipment right on the week boundary, one with different terms — before telling anyone this is solved.
questions.example: Two shipments to the same customer on Monday and Thursday of the same week, both with identical bill-to site, currency, and payment terms, group onto one invoice. A third shipment that week with different payment terms does not group, even though it's the same customer and same week.
commonMistakes: Assuming grouping by exact ship date achieves week-level consolidation
Not recognizing that every attribute in the grouping rule must match, not just the ones the business cares about
Assuming week-level grouping is default out-of-the-box behavior without configuration
Not testing edge cases (week boundaries, mismatched payment terms) before declaring the configuration complete
Confusing grouping rules with pricing or discount rules
keyPoints: Correctly identifies grouping rules as attribute-match based, requiring exact matches on all included attributes
Explains the gap between exact-date grouping and true week-level consolidation
Identifies specific attributes (bill-to site, currency, payment terms) that can silently break grouping
Recommends testing representative edge cases before considering the configuration solved
Communicates the configuration's real limitations clearly rather than overselling it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how AutoInvoice grouping rules work (attribute matching)
Correctly identifies the gap between exact-date and week-level grouping
Identifies specific attributes that can prevent grouping despite correct setup
Recommends appropriate testing before declaring the solution complete

questions.title: Building a Journal Line Rule for a New Payables Accounting Event
questions.prompt: The business wants a new accounting treatment for a 'Payables Invoice' event class: in addition to the standard liability and expense lines, every invoice over $50,000 should generate an extra journal line flagging it to a 'High Value Invoice Tracking' account for internal monitoring, with no change to the invoice's actual liability or expense accounting. Describe how you'd build this using journal line rules and conditions, without disturbing the existing standard lines.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that the existing standard journal line rules (the liability credit and expense debit lines for a Payables Invoice event) should not be modified at all — introducing a new requirement is a case for adding a new, additional journal line rule to the application accounting definition, not editing a working rule and risking regression on existing accounting.

The new journal line rule would be defined with a condition that evaluates the invoice header amount against the $50,000 threshold (a condition on a transaction attribute, similar in mechanism to any other conditional account rule) — if true, the rule fires and produces an additional line using an account rule that resolves to the constant 'High Value Invoice Tracking' account (likely a fixed account value rather than a derived one, since it's a flat monitoring account, not something that varies by supplier or expense category); if the condition is false for an invoice under $50,000, the rule does not fire and no extra line is generated, leaving normal invoices' accounting completely unaffected.

The answer should note this new line needs a balancing consideration — a tracking line that debits or credits an account without an offsetting entry would throw the journal out of balance, so the design must either make this a balanced pair of new lines (an offsetting entry to a suspense or equivalent tracking contra-account) or confirm the accounting method supports an unbalanced informational line in a way the ledger's posting rules accept, which should be validated before this goes to production. The complete answer also stresses testing both an invoice at exactly $50,000 (boundary case) and one just below it, to confirm the condition's boundary (> vs >=) matches the business's actual intent.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd do is leave the existing rules completely alone — the liability and expense lines are working, and editing a working rule to bolt on a new feature is how you introduce a regression on perfectly good invoice accounting. Instead, I'd add a brand new journal line rule to the accounting definition, separate from the existing ones.

That new rule gets a condition checking the invoice amount against $50,000 — same mechanism as any conditional account rule. If it's over the threshold, the rule fires and generates a line pointed at the High Value Invoice Tracking account, which I'd set up as a fixed constant value rather than something derived, since it's one flat monitoring account, not something that changes by supplier or category. If it's under $50,000, the rule just doesn't fire, and every normal invoice's accounting is completely untouched.

The thing I would not skip is the balancing question — if this new line debits or credits something with no offsetting entry, I've just thrown the whole journal out of balance, and that's a real problem, not a cosmetic one. So either this needs to be a balanced pair — an offsetting line to some kind of contra or suspense account — or I need to confirm the ledger's posting rules actually accept an unbalanced informational line, which I wouldn't assume, I'd test it. And I'd specifically test an invoice at exactly $50,000, not just comfortably above or below it, because whether the business means 'over $50,000' as greater-than or greater-than-or-equal is exactly the kind of ambiguity that bites you later if you don't nail it down now.
questions.example: New journal line rule, condition: Invoice Header Amount > 50000 → fires an additional line to 'High Value Invoice Tracking' (fixed account), paired with an offsetting contra-account line to keep the journal balanced. An invoice for $49,999 generates only the standard liability/expense lines; one for $50,001 also generates the tracking pair.
commonMistakes: Editing the existing standard journal line rules instead of adding a new, separate rule
Using a derived account rule for a flat monitoring account instead of a simple fixed/constant value
Forgetting that a new debit or credit line needs a balancing offset or validated unbalanced-line support
Not testing the exact threshold boundary ($50,000 itself) to confirm > vs >= matches business intent
Not confirming the new rule leaves normal invoices' accounting completely unaffected
keyPoints: Adds a new journal line rule rather than modifying the existing standard rules
Correctly uses a condition on invoice amount to control when the rule fires
Uses a fixed/constant account value appropriately for a flat monitoring account
Identifies and addresses the journal-balancing implication of the new line
Tests the exact threshold boundary to confirm correct condition logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly isolates the new requirement into a new, additive journal line rule
Correctly designs the conditional logic and account derivation for the new line
Identifies and addresses the journal-balancing implication
Describes appropriate boundary and regression testing

questions.title: Troubleshooting an Invoice Stuck on a Three-Way Match Hold
questions.prompt: An AP invoice for $8,200 is stuck on a 'Qty Rec Exception' hold even though the receiving clerk insists the full quantity was received and signed for a week ago. Walk through how you'd investigate and resolve this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by not taking either side's claim at face value and going straight to the data: pulling up the PO, the receipt, and the invoice side by side to compare quantities at the line level, not just trusting a summary status. A 'Qty Rec Exception' hold specifically means the matching engine's quantity comparison failed, so the investigation should check whether the receipt was actually entered in the system against the correct PO line, and in the correct unit of measure — a very common real cause is that the clerk received and signed a packing slip physically, but the receipt was never entered in Oracle Fusion, or was entered against the wrong PO line/shipment.

A second common cause to check: the invoice line's unit of measure differs from the PO/receipt's unit of measure (e.g., invoice billed in 'cases' while PO and receipt are in 'each'), which makes quantities appear mismatched even though the underlying physical receipt was correct — this requires checking UOM conversion setup, not assuming a data entry quantity error.

The answer should describe the resolution path once the root cause is identified: if the receipt genuinely wasn't entered, enter it correctly against the right PO line and the hold should clear on the next validation; if it's a UOM mismatch, correct the UOM conversion or the invoice line setup rather than overriding the hold, since manually releasing a quantity hold without fixing the underlying mismatch defeats the control's purpose.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just take the clerk's word for it or assume the system's wrong — I'd pull up the PO, the receipt, and the invoice together and compare them line by line, because a 'Qty Rec Exception' means specifically that the quantity comparison in the match failed, not that something's vaguely broken. My first real guess is that the clerk physically received and signed for it, but nobody actually entered that receipt into Oracle Fusion, or it got entered against the wrong PO line — that happens constantly, a physical signature on a packing slip and a system receipt are two different things.

My second guess, if there is a receipt entered, is a unit of measure mismatch — maybe the PO and receipt are in 'each' and the invoice got entered in 'cases,' so the quantities look wildly different even though physically everything matches. I'd check the UOM setup on both before assuming it's a real quantity discrepancy.

Once I know which one it is, the fix is specific: if the receipt's missing, enter it correctly against the right line and let the hold clear on its own next time it validates. If it's a UOM issue, fix the conversion or the invoice line, don't just manually override the hold — overriding it without fixing the actual mismatch means I've disabled the control instead of solving the problem, and the next invoice with the same root cause will have the same issue.
questions.example: PO line: 500 each. Receipt: entered as 500 each, correctly. Invoice: entered as 10 cases (no UOM conversion configured, system expects 'each'). Fix: correct the invoice line UOM or configure the case-to-each conversion rather than overriding the hold.
commonMistakes: Assuming the clerk's physical sign-off means the receipt was correctly entered in the system
Manually overriding the quantity hold instead of identifying and fixing the root cause
Not checking for a unit-of-measure mismatch between PO, receipt, and invoice
Checking only summary status instead of line-level quantity comparison
Assuming the hold means a genuine quantity discrepancy without verifying receipt entry first
keyPoints: Investigates at the line level comparing PO, receipt, and invoice quantities directly
Identifies missing/misapplied receipt entry as a common root cause
Identifies unit-of-measure mismatch as a second common root cause
Resolves by fixing the root cause rather than manually overriding the hold
Distinguishes a physical sign-off from a system-entered receipt

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly investigates PO/receipt/invoice at the line level rather than relying on summary status
Identifies realistic, specific root causes (missing receipt, UOM mismatch)
Resolves via fixing the root cause rather than overriding the control
Demonstrates sound skepticism of both parties' initial claims

questions.title: A Requisition Stuck in Approval with No Visible Approver
questions.prompt: A requester says their $3,500 requisition has been 'pending approval' for six days with no approver showing in the approval history, and no one on the finance team seems to know who it's waiting on. How do you investigate and resolve this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats a requisition stuck with no visible approver as most likely an approval rule/hierarchy configuration gap, not a person simply ignoring a notification. The investigation should start by checking the requisition's approval history/action log in detail (not just the summary status) to see exactly where the workflow is — whether it's genuinely waiting at a named approver step, or whether the approval chain actually has no resolved approver at that step (a common cause: the requester's manager field is blank, inactive, or the hierarchy used by the approval rule has a gap for this particular requester or amount range).

The answer should name specific likely causes: a change in approval rule configuration (e.g., a new dollar-threshold rule was added recently that doesn't have a defined approver for this specific range or business unit), a supervisor hierarchy gap (the requester's manager was terminated or changed roles and the hierarchy wasn't updated), or the requisition being misrouted due to a business-unit or category mismatch in the rule conditions.

The resolution path should include both an immediate fix (manually identifying and assigning/reassigning an approver so this specific requisition can move, often via an admin action) and a root-cause fix (correcting the approval rule or hierarchy gap so future requisitions in the same category/amount range/business unit don't hit the same dead end) — stopping at the immediate fix without addressing the root cause just defers the same problem to the next requester.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A requisition stuck with literally no approver showing is almost never 'someone's ignoring their inbox' — that's a configuration gap in the approval hierarchy or rules, and I'd investigate it that way from the start. First I'd pull the full approval action history, not just the pending status, to see exactly where in the chain it's stuck — is it actually sitting with a named person, or is the chain itself broken with nobody resolved at this step?

The usual suspects: the requester's manager field is blank or points to someone who's inactive or changed roles and nobody updated the hierarchy; or there's a dollar-threshold approval rule that got added or changed recently and doesn't actually have a defined approver for this specific range or business unit; or the requisition's category or business unit doesn't match any rule condition cleanly, so it's routing nowhere.

Once I find the actual gap, I'd do two things, not just one. Short term, I'd manually assign or reassign an approver so this specific requisition can move today — the requester's been waiting six days, that's a real business impact. But I wouldn't stop there — I'd fix the actual rule or hierarchy gap, because if I only fix this one requisition, the next person who hits that same amount range or business unit combination is going to land in the exact same dead end next week.
questions.example: A new $2,500+ approval rule was added for the Marketing business unit but no approver was assigned for amounts between $3,000-$5,000 specifically — the requisition routes into that gap and has no resolvable next approver. Fix: assign the missing approver tier and manually route the stuck requisition.
commonMistakes: Assuming the delay is due to an approver ignoring notifications rather than investigating a configuration gap
Checking only the summary 'pending' status instead of the detailed approval action history
Fixing only this one requisition without addressing the underlying rule/hierarchy gap
Not considering a blank or inactive supervisor hierarchy entry as a root cause
Not considering a mismatched business unit/category condition as a routing cause
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses a no-approver situation as a likely rule/hierarchy configuration gap
Investigates the detailed approval action history, not just summary status
Identifies specific, realistic root causes (hierarchy gap, rule threshold gap, category/BU mismatch)
Provides both an immediate fix and a root-cause fix
Recognizes the business impact of the delay while still fixing the real cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the likely root cause category (rule/hierarchy gap)
Describes a thorough investigation using detailed approval history
Provides both an immediate fix and a root-cause fix
Identifies realistic, specific causes rather than generic troubleshooting

questions.title: A Receipt Accrual That Never Reversed
questions.prompt: The GL shows a receipt accrual liability account with a growing, unreversed balance going back eight months, even though the corresponding AP invoices were all paid long ago. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains the expected mechanics first, to frame the diagnosis: a receipt accrual (common for expense/period-end accruals and standard for inventory items) books an estimated liability at receipt, which should reverse automatically once the matched AP invoice is validated and accounted — the invoice accounting effectively replaces the estimated accrual with the actual liability. A growing, unreversed balance means that reversal step is not completing for a subset of transactions, not that accruals are inherently broken.

The investigation should pull the specific receipts contributing to the unreversed balance and check, for each, whether a matching AP invoice was actually ever created and accounted against that same PO/receipt, or whether the invoice was entered but matched to a different PO line/distribution than the one the accrual was booked against — a mismatch here is a common, specific cause: the accrual and the eventual invoice accounting end up on different PO shipment lines, so neither one 'sees' the other to trigger a reversal. Another specific cause: the receipt accrual process (e.g., the periodic accrual reconciliation/clearing process) that's supposed to run and perform the reversal wasn't actually scheduled or has been failing silently for months, which is worth checking directly rather than assuming every individual transaction has its own problem.

The resolution should include correcting the specific stuck transactions (re-matching, or manually processing the applicable reversal/write-off with appropriate review and approval since this touches real GL balances) and verifying the scheduled accrual reconciliation process is actually running going forward, since an eight-month gap strongly suggests a systemic process failure, not eight months of coincidental one-off errors.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First I'd make sure I actually understand what's supposed to happen before I go looking for what's broken: a receipt accrual books an estimated liability when goods are received, and that's supposed to reverse once the real AP invoice gets matched and accounted against that same receipt — the real invoice accounting effectively takes over from the estimate. So an eight-month growing, unreversed balance tells me that handoff isn't happening for some set of transactions, not that accruals themselves are broken.

I'd pull the specific receipts behind that growing balance and check each one: was an invoice ever actually created and accounted against that exact PO and receipt? A really common, specific cause is that the invoice got matched to a different PO shipment line or distribution than the one the accrual was booked against — so from the system's point of view, neither side ever actually connects to trigger a reversal, even though logically they're the same transaction. The other thing I'd check directly, not assume: is the scheduled accrual reconciliation or clearing process that's supposed to handle this even running? Eight months of growth smells more like a process that silently stopped running than eight months of unrelated one-off mismatches.

For the fix, I'd correct the specific stuck transactions — re-matching where that's the issue, or a reviewed, approved manual adjustment where re-matching isn't possible — and separately confirm that scheduled process is actually running going forward, because fixing the historical balance without fixing the process just means I'm back here in another eight months.
questions.example: Receipt R-4471 booked an accrual against PO line 3. The invoice for that PO was later matched to PO line 4 instead of line 3 due to a data entry error — the accrual for line 3 never reverses because no invoice accounting is ever recorded against line 3 specifically.
commonMistakes: Assuming the accrual mechanism itself is broken rather than investigating a reversal/matching gap
Not checking whether invoices were matched to the correct PO line/distribution the accrual was booked against
Not verifying whether the scheduled accrual reconciliation process is actually running
Treating eight months of growth as unrelated one-off errors rather than suspecting a systemic process failure
Fixing the historical balance without confirming the underlying process is corrected going forward
keyPoints: Correctly explains the expected accrual-to-reversal mechanism before diagnosing the failure
Investigates specific receipts for PO line/distribution matching mismatches
Checks whether the scheduled accrual reconciliation process is actually running
Distinguishes systemic process failure from isolated transaction errors given the time span
Provides both a correction for historical balances and a fix for ongoing process health

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the expected accrual/reversal mechanism as a diagnostic baseline
Identifies realistic, specific root causes (PO line mismatch, failed scheduled process)
Distinguishes systemic failure from isolated errors given the time span
Provides both historical correction and forward-looking process fix

questions.title: Invoice Holds That Won't Clear After a PO Change Order
questions.prompt: A PO's unit price was corrected from $50 to $45 via a change order after the supplier pointed out an error. Two invoices already matched to the original PO price are now stuck on price holds, and the AP clerk can't figure out why since the invoices were originally within tolerance. Diagnose and resolve this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains the mechanism causing this, which is logical rather than a system bug: matching tolerance is evaluated against the PO's current price at the time matching/validation runs, not the price that was in effect when the invoice was originally entered or first matched. Once the change order updated the PO unit price from $50 to $45, any invoice still carrying the original $50 price is now being compared against a $45 PO price, and a roughly 11% variance likely exceeds a typical tight price tolerance — so invoices that were fine under the old PO price are now out of tolerance under the new one, even though nothing about the invoices themselves changed.

The investigation should confirm this is exactly what happened (check the PO change order history and timing against when the invoices were entered/matched) rather than assuming a random system fault, and should also check whether the change order was intended to apply retroactively to already-matched invoices or only to future POs/shipments going forward — this is a business decision, not just a technical one, and affects the correct resolution.

The resolution should involve correcting the two invoices to reflect the corrected $45 price (if the business intends the price correction to apply to them) — which may mean a credit memo from the supplier for the $5/unit overbilling and a corrected invoice, or an adjustment depending on company policy — rather than simply overriding the price hold, since overriding would pay the invoices at the old, now-known-to-be-incorrect $50 price.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This isn't random — it's actually working exactly as designed, just not in a way the clerk expected. Matching tolerance compares the invoice price against whatever the PO's current price is at the moment it validates, not whatever the PO price was back when the invoice was first entered. Once that change order dropped the PO from $50 to $45, those two invoices, still carrying the old $50 price, are now being compared against $45 — that's roughly an 11% gap, which is well outside a normal tight price tolerance. Nothing about the invoices changed; the goalpost moved.

First thing I'd confirm is the timing — pull the change order history and line it up against when those invoices were entered, just to be sure that's actually what happened rather than assuming it. Then there's a real business question to settle before I touch anything: does the business want this $5 correction applied retroactively to invoices that already matched at the old price, or was the change order only meant to apply going forward to new POs and shipments? That's not my call to make unilaterally.

Assuming the business wants the correction applied, I wouldn't just override the price hold and let the invoices pay at the old $50 — that pays a price everyone now agrees was wrong. I'd get the supplier to issue a credit for the $5/unit overbilling, or process a corrected invoice, depending on what the company's policy is for handling this kind of correction, so the actual payment reflects the price everyone's agreed is correct.
questions.example: PO price corrected from $50 to $45 via change order on 10/5. Invoice #A, entered 9/28 at $50/unit, re-validates on 10/6 and compares against the now-$45 PO price — an 11% variance exceeds a 2% tolerance, generating a price hold even though the invoice was within tolerance when first matched.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is a random system glitch rather than the expected effect of tolerance comparing against the current PO price
Overriding the price hold and paying at the old, now-incorrect price instead of resolving the underlying discrepancy
Not checking whether the change order was intended to apply retroactively to already-matched invoices
Not confirming the timing/causal link between the change order and the holds before proposing a fix
Treating this as purely a technical fix without recognizing the business decision involved
keyPoints: Correctly explains that tolerance compares against the PO's current price, not the price at original match time
Confirms the causal link via change order history and timing before proposing a fix
Identifies the retroactive-vs-forward-only business decision as part of the resolution
Resolves via correcting the invoices (credit/adjustment) rather than overriding the hold
Demonstrates understanding that a system behaving as designed can still surprise users

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the tolerance-vs-current-PO-price mechanism as the root cause
Confirms the causal link via investigation rather than assumption
Identifies the retroactive application business decision as part of the resolution
Resolves appropriately without simply overriding the hold at the incorrect price

questions.title: A Batch of Sales Orders Failing AutoInvoice
questions.prompt: Overnight, AutoInvoice ran and 340 of 1,200 fulfilled sales order lines failed to become invoices, all for the same customer. The business is asking why their biggest customer's invoices didn't go out. Walk through your diagnostic approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by going to the AutoInvoice exception/error report for the run rather than guessing, since the process logs a specific rejection reason per failed line, and the fact that all failures share one customer is itself a strong diagnostic clue pointing toward something specific to that customer's setup rather than a random or systemic failure (which would more likely be spread across customers).

The answer should name the most likely customer-specific causes to check first, in rough likelihood order: the customer's bill-to site was recently changed, end-dated, or made inactive, so lines referencing the old site can no longer resolve; a customer-specific price list or payment terms assignment is missing or was end-dated; or a credit hold was placed on the customer account between fulfillment and the AutoInvoice run, which can block invoice creation even for already-fulfilled lines. The exception report should directly state which of these it is in most cases, since AutoInvoice errors are typically specific (e.g., 'Bill-To Site is invalid') rather than generic.

The resolution should address the root cause (reactivating/correcting the site or price list assignment, or resolving the credit hold per policy) and then resubmit only the failed lines through AutoInvoice — not the full batch — to avoid re-processing the 860 lines that already succeeded, followed by confirming with the business whether the delay has any customer-facing financial impact (e.g., late payment terms starting from invoice date) that needs separate communication.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't guess at this — I'd go straight to the AutoInvoice exception report for that run, because it logs a specific reason for every single rejected line, not just 'failed.' The fact that all 340 failures are the same customer is actually useful information on its own — that pattern points at something specific to that customer's setup, not a random system issue, which would more likely be scattered across different customers instead of concentrated on one.

My short list of what to check, in order of how often I've actually seen this: did something change on that customer's bill-to site recently — end-dated, made inactive, address change — so lines referencing the old site can't resolve anymore? Is there a price list or payment terms assignment for this customer that's missing or expired? And did a credit hold get placed on this customer's account sometime between when these lines fulfilled and when AutoInvoice ran — that can block invoice creation even on stuff that already shipped. The exception report usually just tells you directly which of these it is, in plain language like 'Bill-To Site is invalid,' so I'm not actually guessing blind here.

Once I know the actual cause, I fix that — reactivate the site, fix the price list assignment, resolve the credit hold through whatever the actual policy is — and then I resubmit just the 340 failed lines, not the whole 1,200-line batch, since the other 860 already succeeded and don't need to run again. And I'd flag to the business separately whether this delay has any real financial consequence, like payment terms counting from invoice date, since that's a business conversation, not just a technical fix.
questions.example: AutoInvoice exception report shows all 340 failed lines with the error 'Bill-To Site is invalid' — the customer's bill-to site was end-dated three days earlier during an unrelated data cleanup. Fix: reactivate or correct the site reference, then resubmit only the 340 affected lines.

Not recognizing the single-customer pattern as a diagnostic clue pointing to customer-specific setup
Resubmitting the entire 1,200-line batch instead of only the 340 failed lines
Not checking for a credit hold placed between fulfillment and the AutoInvoice run
Fixing the technical cause without flagging potential business/financial impact of the delay

Flags potential business impact of the delay separately from the technical fix
