questions.title: Designing Customer Data to Support Both Sales and Billing Needs
questions.prompt: A client's sales team wants to track multiple contacts and relationships per customer (decision makers, influencers, site contacts), while the billing team only cares about a single valid bill-to address and payment terms per customer account. How does the Trading Community Model support both needs without creating two disconnected sets of customer data?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that the Trading Community Model (TCM) is built specifically to support exactly this kind of layered need: a single party record represents the customer organization as one entity, with separate, related structures for sites/addresses (including a designation of which site serves as the default bill-to for billing purposes) and for contacts/relationships (the people associated with that party, each potentially tagged with their role — decision maker, influencer, site contact), all linked back to the same underlying party rather than existing as disconnected records.

The answer should explain that this means sales and billing are drawing from the same customer data, not two separate systems: the sales team's view of multiple contacts and relationships is additional structure built on top of the same party record billing is using, not a parallel, disconnected customer master — billing simply queries for the designated bill-to site and payment terms associated with the party, while sales can query the full set of contacts and relationships for the same party without those two views ever needing to be reconciled against each other, because they were never separate in the first place.

A complete answer would note the practical design implication: when implementing this, it's important to actually designate and maintain which site is the bill-to default (rather than leaving every address ambiguous) and which contacts carry which roles, since TCM's flexibility to support rich relationship data doesn't automatically mean every team configures and maintains their specific slice of it correctly — the model supports both needs, but someone still has to maintain the billing-relevant designations correctly for billing to actually work smoothly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The Trading Community Model is actually built for exactly this kind of layered requirement — it's not that sales and billing need two different systems, it's that they're both looking at different facets of the same underlying party record. The customer organization is one party. On top of that, there are sites and addresses, one of which gets designated as the default bill-to for billing purposes, and separately there are contacts and relationships — the people tied to that party, each one taggable with a role like decision maker, influencer, or site contact.

So when I explain this to the client, the key point is that sales and billing aren't working off two disconnected sets of customer data that need to somehow stay in sync — they're both querying the same party record, just pulling different slices of it. Billing just needs the designated bill-to site and payment terms for that party. Sales pulls the full set of contacts and relationships for that same party. Neither team's view needs to be reconciled against the other's, because there was never a second, separate customer master to begin with.

The thing I would flag as a real implementation task, though: this flexibility doesn't maintain itself. Someone actually has to designate which site is the bill-to default and make sure it stays correct, and someone has to actually tag contacts with the right roles. The model supports both needs beautifully, but that doesn't mean it happens automatically — if nobody maintains those billing-relevant designations, billing is going to have a bad time even though the underlying data model was never the problem.
questions.example: Party 'Acme Corp': one party record, with Site A designated as the default bill-to (billing queries this), and three contacts linked to the same party — a Decision Maker, an Influencer, and a Site Contact (sales queries these) — all tied to the same underlying party, not separate customer records.
commonMistakes: Describing sales and billing as needing two separate customer data structures
Not explaining that sites/addresses and contacts/relationships both link back to the same party record
Not mentioning the bill-to default designation as the specific mechanism billing relies on
Assuming the data model's flexibility means correct designations happen automatically without maintenance
Not explaining how contact roles (decision maker, influencer, site contact) are represented
keyPoints: Correctly explains the Trading Community Model's party-centric structure
Explains sites/addresses (with bill-to designation) and contacts/relationships as linked facets of one party
Explains how sales and billing draw from the same underlying data without needing reconciliation
Identifies the practical need to actively maintain billing-relevant designations
Demonstrates accurate understanding of TCM's role/relationship tagging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Trading Community Model's party-centric design
Correctly connects sales (contacts/relationships) and billing (bill-to site) to the same party
Explains why this avoids disconnected/duplicated customer data
Flags the practical maintenance responsibility for correct designations

questions.title: Designing a Self-Service Reporting Layer Without Exposing Raw Tables
questions.prompt: A client's finance team wants to let a handful of trained power users write their own ad-hoc queries against Oracle Fusion financial data for custom analysis, but you're concerned about giving them direct access to raw application tables. How would you architect a layer that gives them real querying power without the risks of raw table access?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains the specific risks of raw table access that motivate a different design: raw application tables are often normalized in ways that require understanding many non-obvious joins and status/lifecycle columns correctly to avoid wrong results (as covered in reading table/view documentation), they can include sensitive columns irrelevant to the analysis need, and granting direct query access to production application tables used by the live transactional system risks both accidental performance impact on production processing and, more subtly, someone writing a plausible-looking but subtly incorrect query that produces a confidently wrong answer no one catches.

The recommended design is an intermediate reporting/semantic layer — views (or a dedicated reporting schema/subject area, depending on available tooling) that pre-join the common, correct relationships (the specific risky joins already resolved correctly once, by someone who understands the data model deeply), expose only business-relevant columns with clear, business-friendly naming, and can be built against a reporting replica or read-only reporting structure rather than the live transactional tables directly, isolating any query load from production processing.

The answer should frame this as the standard way to give real power to trained users without the raw-access risk: power users still get genuine flexibility to slice, filter, and combine this pre-joined, curated layer in their own ad-hoc ways, which is the actual thing they're asking for, while the organization retains control over the parts of the data model that are genuinely easy to get wrong, rather than either refusing them access entirely (blocking a legitimate need) or granting unrestricted raw access (accepting an unmanaged risk).
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd be concerned about raw table access for specific, concrete reasons, not just a vague sense of risk. The application tables are normalized in ways that require knowing a lot of non-obvious joins and status columns to get right — get one of those wrong and you get a plausible-looking, confidently wrong number that nobody catches, which is honestly worse than an obvious error. There's also sensitive data in some of those tables that has nothing to do with what these power users are actually trying to analyze, and letting ad-hoc queries run directly against production transactional tables risks actually slowing down the live system these queries weren't meant to touch.

So what I'd build instead is a reporting layer in between — views, or a dedicated reporting schema if the tooling supports it, that pre-join the tricky relationships correctly once, expose only the columns that actually matter for this kind of analysis with clear business-friendly names, and ideally sit on a reporting replica rather than the live transactional tables directly, so none of this ad-hoc querying touches production processing at all.

The way I'd frame this to the client: this isn't about restricting their power users, it's about giving them real flexibility to slice and combine data however they want on top of a layer that's already correct, instead of either blocking them entirely or handing them unrestricted raw access and hoping nobody writes a bad join. They get the actual thing they're asking for — genuine ad-hoc power — and the organization keeps control over exactly the parts of the data model that are easiest to get wrong.
questions.example: A reporting view 'RPT_AP_INVOICE_SUMMARY' pre-joins AP_INVOICES, AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS, and supplier/site tables correctly, exposing clean business column names (supplier_name, invoice_status_display) on a reporting replica — power users query this view freely rather than the raw, normalized application tables.
commonMistakes: Granting unrestricted raw table access to satisfy the ad-hoc querying request
Refusing any self-service access at all rather than designing a safe intermediate layer
Not identifying the specific risks of raw access (non-obvious joins, sensitive columns, production performance impact)
Building the reporting layer directly against live transactional tables instead of a reporting replica
Not framing the design as preserving real querying flexibility rather than just restricting access
keyPoints: Identifies specific, concrete risks of raw table access rather than a vague concern
Proposes a curated reporting/semantic layer (views or reporting schema) as the solution
Recommends isolating this layer from production transactional load via a reporting replica
Frames the design as preserving genuine power-user flexibility, not just restricting access
Explains how pre-joining resolves the error-prone complexity for users

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies specific, concrete risks of raw table access
Proposes a sound intermediate reporting/semantic layer design
Recommends isolating query load from production via a reporting replica
Frames the solution as enabling real flexibility, not just restriction

questions.title: Justifying an FBDI-Based Load Approach to a Skeptical Client Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A client's finance director is skeptical of your proposal to migrate 20,000 historical AP records using FBDI, saying 'that sounds like a script is just dumping data in, I don't trust that as much as having my team enter it manually so we know it's right.' How do you respond and build her confidence in the approach?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer takes the finance director's underlying concern seriously rather than dismissing it as a misunderstanding of the technology — her real worry is accuracy and control, and manual entry feels safer to her because it feels more deliberate, even though it is actually far more error-prone at 20,000 records. The response should reframe the comparison honestly: manual entry of 20,000 records means 20,000 individual opportunities for a typo, a transposed digit, or a missed field, performed by tired humans under deadline pressure, with no systematic validation beyond whatever the data-entry screen itself enforces — FBDI, by contrast, applies the exact same validation rules to every single row, consistently, and produces an explicit rejection report for anything that doesn't pass, which is actually more rigorous and auditable than manual entry, not less.

The answer should propose concrete trust-building steps rather than just asserting FBDI is better: running a small test batch first and showing her the validation/rejection report so she can see the control in action, reconciling the final loaded totals against the legacy system's totals (count and dollar amount) so there's a verifiable tie-out she can review herself, and offering her team a role in the process — reviewing the populated templates before upload, or spot-checking a sample of loaded records — so this isn't a black box she has no visibility into, but a controlled process she can audit at multiple points.

The answer should close by acknowledging that her skepticism is a reasonable, protective instinct for someone accountable for the accuracy of 20,000 financial records, and that earning her trust through demonstrated control is the right response, not persuading her to simply take it on faith.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't treat her concern as a misunderstanding of the technology — I think she's actually worried about the right thing, accuracy and control, she's just assuming manual entry gives her more of both, and at 20,000 records that's actually backwards. I'd tell her directly: manual entry of 20,000 records means 20,000 separate chances for a typo or a transposed number, done by people who are tired and under deadline pressure, with basically no systematic check beyond whatever the entry screen itself catches. FBDI applies the exact same validation to every single row, consistently, and hands you an explicit list of anything that failed — that's actually more rigorous and more auditable than manual entry, not less, even though it feels less hands-on.

But I wouldn't just assert that and expect her to take my word for it. I'd propose running a small test batch first and literally showing her the validation report, so she sees the control working with her own eyes instead of just hearing me describe it. I'd reconcile the final loaded totals against the legacy system's totals, both count and dollar amount, so there's something concrete she or her team can actually check. And I'd offer her team a real role in this — reviewing the populated templates before we upload anything, or spot-checking a sample of what loaded — so it's not a black box she has no visibility into.

I'd end by telling her honestly that her instinct to be cautious with 20,000 financial records is exactly the right instinct for someone in her seat — I'm not trying to talk her out of being careful, I'm trying to show her a way to get that same level of control with a method that's actually safer at this volume than the one she's defaulting to.
questions.example: Test batch of 50 records run first, validation report reviewed with the finance director; full load's final count and dollar total reconciled against the legacy system's export before sign-off; her team spot-checks 20 randomly selected loaded invoices against source documents.

Simply asserting FBDI is 'more accurate' without proposing concrete, verifiable trust-building steps
Not offering her team a visible role or checkpoint in the process
Not proposing reconciliation against the legacy system's totals as a verification step
Failing to acknowledge her skepticism as a reasonable instinct rather than an obstacle to overcome

Explains concretely why manual entry at this volume is actually more error-prone than FBDI
Proposes a test batch and validation report review as a concrete trust-building step
Proposes reconciliation against legacy totals and team spot-checking for verifiable control
Acknowledges her skepticism as reasonable rather than something to talk her out of

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Consultant Through a Failed Subledger Reconciliation
questions.prompt: A junior consultant on your team spent two days trying to reconcile a subledger-to-GL variance and comes to you frustrated, saying 'I've checked everything three times, the numbers just don't match and I don't know what else to try.' How do you coach them through this rather than just solving it yourself?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer resists the temptation to simply take over and solve the problem directly, which would resolve this one instance but teach the junior consultant nothing transferable for the next variance they hit. Instead, the response should walk them through a structured diagnostic approach by asking questions rather than supplying answers: what exactly has been checked three times (often 'checking everything three times' means re-verifying the same narrow thing repeatedly rather than genuinely covering different possible causes), what the actual size and pattern of the variance is (a flat, consistent dollar amount suggests something different than a variance that grows with volume), and whether they've isolated the variance to a specific period, transaction type, or event class versus looking at an aggregate total that could be masking several offsetting issues.

The answer should describe guiding them toward specific, concrete next diagnostic steps appropriate to subledger-to-GL reconciliation specifically: checking whether all expected accounting events actually reached 'Accounted' status, checking whether everything accounted was actually transferred and posted to GL (a common, specific gap), and checking for a recent account rule or mapping set change that could explain a variance appearing at a specific point in time — guiding them to try one specific, falsifiable hypothesis at a time rather than re-checking broadly and vaguely.

The answer should close by framing this explicitly as a teaching moment: explaining out loud why each diagnostic question matters, not just what to check next, so the junior consultant builds a repeatable mental model for subledger reconciliation troubleshooting generally, and checking in afterward on how the approach worked rather than disappearing once pointed in a direction.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My instinct is not to just take this and solve it myself, because that fixes today's problem and teaches them nothing for the next one. So I'd start by asking questions instead of handing over answers. First: what specifically have you checked three times? A lot of the time 'I checked everything three times' actually means re-verifying the same narrow thing over and over, not genuinely covering different possible causes — so I want to know the actual scope of what's been ruled out.

Then I'd ask about the shape of the variance itself — is it a flat, consistent dollar amount, or does it grow with volume? Those point in different directions. And have they isolated this to a specific period or transaction type, or are they looking at one aggregate total that could actually be hiding two or three offsetting issues canceling each other out partially?

From there I'd walk them toward specific next steps rather than 'go check more stuff' — did everything that should have an accounting event actually reach Accounted status, did everything that's Accounted actually get transferred and posted to GL, which is a really common and specific gap people miss, and was there any recent change to an account rule or mapping set that lines up with when this variance started appearing. I'd push them to test one specific, falsifiable idea at a time instead of re-checking broadly and vaguely, which is clearly what's happened over the last two days.

And I'd explain out loud why each of these questions matters, not just tell them what to go click on next, because the actual goal here is them walking away with a repeatable way to think through the next subledger variance themselves — and I'd check back in later, not just point them in a direction and disappear.
questions.example: Coaching question sequence: 'What have you actually ruled out vs. re-checked? Is the variance flat or does it scale with volume? Have you confirmed everything Accounted actually transferred to GL? Did anything change on the account rules around when this started?' — leads the junior consultant to discover a batch of transactions stuck in 'Accounted' but never transferred.
commonMistakes: Taking over and solving the variance directly instead of coaching the junior consultant through it
Not probing what 'checked three times' actually covered versus repeated narrow checking
Giving a list of things to check without explaining why each one matters
Not distinguishing accounted-but-not-transferred as a specific, common gap to check
Disappearing after pointing them in a direction instead of following up on the outcome
keyPoints: Coaches through questions rather than solving the problem directly
Probes what was actually checked versus repeatedly re-verified
Guides toward specific, falsifiable diagnostic hypotheses (accounted vs. transferred, rule changes)
Explains the reasoning behind each diagnostic step, not just the step itself
Follows up afterward rather than abandoning the junior consultant once redirected

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Coaches through questions rather than directly solving the problem
Proposes specific, accurate diagnostic steps relevant to subledger reconciliation
Explains reasoning to build the junior consultant's transferable skill
Includes appropriate follow-up rather than one-time redirection

questions.title: Negotiating Scope on an Ambiguous P2P Configuration Request
questions.prompt: A client's procurement director asks you to 'set up approval routing that makes sense for our organization' with no further detail, and expects it done by the end of the week. How do you handle this ambiguous, time-pressured request without either guessing at requirements or stalling the project waiting for perfect clarity?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer avoids both failure modes named in the question: guessing at requirements and building something that may not match the organization's actual approval needs (risking significant rework), and stalling the project by refusing to proceed until every detail is specified (which isn't realistic for a client who may not know what they don't know yet, and damages the relationship by appearing unhelpful or overly rigid).

The recommended approach is a short, structured requirements conversation that fits inside the timeline rather than extending it: coming back to the procurement director with a small set of specific, concrete questions that get at the real decision points behind 'approval routing that makes sense' — what dollar thresholds should trigger escalation to higher approval tiers, whether routing should differ by purchasing category (capital vs. expense, for example), whether there are specific individuals whose purchases need different handling (e.g., the CFO's own purchases), and whether multiple business units need different hierarchies or one hierarchy serves everyone. This should take a focused 30-45 minute conversation, not an extended discovery phase, and can often happen the same day.

The answer should describe proposing a specific starting design based on that conversation's answers, explicitly presented as a draft for the director's review and adjustment rather than a finished deliverable — this gets something concrete in front of the client by the end of the week as promised, while building in an explicit checkpoint for refinement rather than presenting a guess as if it were confirmed to be correct. The complete answer should frame this as faster, not slower, than either guessing or stalling, since a wrong guess reviewed and corrected later costs more total time than a short clarifying conversation up front.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just guess at this, and I also wouldn't go back and say 'I need way more detail before I can start' — both of those are bad options here. Guessing risks building something that doesn't actually match how this organization makes decisions, which means real rework later. Stalling for perfect clarity isn't realistic either — she may genuinely not know yet what she doesn't know, and it makes me look unhelpful right when she needs something delivered.

What I'd actually do is go back to her with a short, specific set of questions, not an open-ended 'tell me everything' ask — something I can get through in thirty or forty-five minutes, same day if possible. What dollar thresholds should trigger escalation to a higher approval tier? Does routing need to differ by category, say capital versus expense purchases? Are there specific people, like the CFO, whose own purchases need different handling? Does this need to be one hierarchy for everyone, or do different business units need their own?

From there, I'd build a specific starting design based on her answers and bring it to her explicitly as a draft for review, not a finished, locked-in deliverable — that gets her something real and concrete by end of week like she asked for, but it's framed honestly as 'here's a starting point, tell me what to adjust' rather than me quietly guessing and hoping it's right. Honestly, that short conversation up front is faster overall than either extreme — a wrong guess that needs correcting later costs more total time than forty-five minutes of the right questions now.
questions.example: Quick clarifying call: 'What dollar threshold needs VP approval? Does capital spend route differently than expense? Any individuals who need special handling?' Draft approval hierarchy delivered Friday, explicitly labeled as a starting point for her review and adjustment, not a final configuration.
commonMistakes: Guessing at approval routing requirements without any clarifying conversation
Stalling the project by insisting on exhaustive requirements before starting any work
Asking an open-ended 'tell me everything' question instead of a short, specific set of decision-point questions
Presenting a first-draft design as a finished deliverable rather than explicitly inviting adjustment
Not meeting the stated timeline because of unnecessary extended discovery
keyPoints: Avoids both guessing at requirements and stalling for perfect clarity
Proposes a short, specific, time-boxed clarifying conversation
Asks concrete questions targeting the real decision points behind the vague request
Delivers a draft design within the timeline, explicitly framed as open to adjustment
Frames the approach as faster overall than either extreme

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both guessing and stalling as failure modes
Proposes a short, specific, time-boxed clarifying conversation with concrete questions
Delivers within the timeline via a draft explicitly open to adjustment
Articulates why this approach is efficient, not just safe

questions.title: Owning an Incident Where a Bad FBDI Import Corrupted GL Balances
questions.prompt: You ran an FBDI journal import that you believed was fully tested, but a mapping error caused 300 journal lines to post to the wrong cost centers, and this wasn't discovered until two weeks later during a management review, after the period had already closed. How do you handle owning this incident with the client?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with direct, specific accountability rather than deflecting to the testing process, the client's review process, or bad luck — the candidate ran the import and should own that the testing was insufficient to catch this specific mapping error, stated plainly and without excessive self-flagellation that derails the conversation into reassuring the consultant rather than fixing the problem. The communication to the client should be prompt, factual, and specific: exactly what happened (which cost centers were affected, how many lines, what dollar amount), how it was discovered, and — critically — a concrete remediation plan, not just an apology.

The remediation plan should address both the immediate correction (since the period is already closed, this likely requires formal journal reclassification entries in a current or catch-up period, following whatever the client's close correction policy requires, rather than attempting to quietly 'fix' historical closed-period data) and the process gap that allowed this to go undetected for two weeks (proposing a specific improvement — such as a post-import reconciliation check comparing posted amounts by cost center against expected source totals — that would have caught this mapping error before close, not just promising to 'be more careful').

The answer should also address the trust-repair dimension explicitly: being transparent that this was a real process gap, not just an unlucky one-off, and proactively offering to review other recent imports for the same category of risk — demonstrating that the response to this incident is systemic, not just a fix for this one instance, which is what actually rebuilds a client's confidence after a real financial error.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd own this directly and specifically, not vaguely. I ran that import, and whatever testing I did wasn't enough to catch this particular mapping error — that's just true, and I'd say it that plainly to the client rather than drowning the conversation in self-criticism that ends up making them reassure me instead of focusing on fixing the actual problem.

What I'd bring to them is specific and factual: exactly which cost centers got hit, how many lines, what dollar amount, how it got discovered. And critically, I wouldn't show up with just an apology — I'd show up with an actual remediation plan. Since the period's already closed, this almost certainly means a formal journal reclassification in a current or catch-up period, following whatever their actual close-correction policy requires — I'm not going to try to quietly patch closed-period data and pretend this didn't happen.

Then I'd address the actual gap that let this sit undetected for two weeks, because 'I'll be more careful next time' isn't a real answer to that. I'd propose something concrete — a post-import reconciliation check that compares posted amounts by cost center against the expected source totals, something that would have caught this specific error before close instead of relying on someone noticing it in a management review two weeks later.

And I'd be upfront that this was a real gap in my process, not just bad luck, and I'd proactively offer to go back and review other recent imports for this same category of risk — because the thing that actually rebuilds trust after something like this isn't just fixing this one incident, it's showing them the response is systemic, not a one-off patch.
questions.example: Disclosure to client: '300 journal lines totaling $184,000 posted to the wrong cost center due to a mapping set error in the Oct 3 import, discovered during your Oct 17 management review. Remediation: formal reclassification entries in the current period per your close correction policy, plus a new post-import reconciliation check I'll add to catch this category of error before future closes. I'd also like to review the prior three imports for the same risk.'
commonMistakes: Deflecting blame to the testing process, the client's review timing, or circumstances rather than owning it directly
Leading with an apology without a concrete remediation plan
Attempting to quietly correct closed-period data instead of following proper reclassification/correction procedure
Promising only to 'be more careful' instead of proposing a specific process improvement
Not proactively offering to review other recent work for the same category of risk
keyPoints: Owns the incident directly and specifically without deflecting
Communicates factually and specifically about what happened and its impact
Proposes a concrete remediation plan addressing the closed-period correction properly
Identifies a specific process improvement, not just a promise to be more careful
Proactively offers to review other work for the same category of risk to rebuild trust

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Owns the incident directly and specifically without deflection
Proposes a correct, concrete remediation plan for the closed-period correction
Identifies a specific, concrete process improvement
Demonstrates genuine trust-repair behavior (proactive review offer)

questions.title: Presenting an Integration Design Decision to a Steering Committee
questions.prompt: You've decided to recommend an event-driven integration design over a simpler polling-based one for a client's banking integration, which costs more upfront but is more robust. You need to present and defend this to a project steering committee that includes non-technical executives focused on budget and timeline. How do you present this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer translates the technical tradeoff into business terms the committee actually cares about — budget, timeline, and risk — rather than presenting it as a technical preference. The presentation should lead with the business consequence of each option: the polling approach costs less upfront and is faster to build, but introduces an ongoing operational risk (payment status visibility delayed by the polling interval, which has a concrete business impact if that delay affects cash positioning decisions or customer-facing payment confirmation) and a maintenance cost that accrues over time rather than being paid once.

The event-driven approach costs more upfront specifically because of described, concrete work (the banking partner needs to expose/consume a notification endpoint, requiring coordination and testing), but should be framed in terms of what that additional cost buys: near-real-time status visibility and lower long-term operational overhead, not an abstract 'better architecture' claim that gives the committee nothing to actually weigh.

The answer should present this as a genuine decision with a clear recommendation, not an unresolved technical debate dumped on the committee to adjudicate — stating the recommended option clearly, showing the cost/timeline delta in concrete numbers (dollars, days) alongside the risk/benefit tradeoff, and inviting the committee's input on whether the business risk of delayed status visibility is acceptable given their priorities, which is genuinely their call to make, not a technical question — while being prepared to implement either decision professionally once the committee decides, since the recommendation does not override their authority over the actual budget and risk tradeoff.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't present this as a technical debate — I'd translate it straight into the terms this committee actually cares about: budget, timeline, and risk. So I'd lead with the business consequence of each option, not the architecture itself. Polling is cheaper and faster to build, but it carries an ongoing risk — payment status visibility is delayed by however long the polling interval is, and that has a real business impact if it affects cash positioning decisions or how fast you can confirm a payment to a customer. It's also a cost that keeps accruing over time rather than being paid once.

The event-driven option costs more upfront for a specific, concrete reason — the banking partner needs to expose and consume a notification endpoint, which means coordination and testing work on both sides. I'd frame that extra cost in terms of exactly what it buys: near-real-time status visibility and lower ongoing operational overhead, not some vague claim that it's 'more robust,' which doesn't give a room full of executives anything they can actually weigh against a budget number.

And I wouldn't dump this on them as an open technical debate for them to adjudicate — I'd give them a clear recommendation, show the actual cost and timeline delta in dollars and days, and then genuinely ask them: is the business risk of delayed status visibility acceptable given your priorities right now? That's actually their call, not a technical question I should be making unilaterally for them. And whichever way they decide, I'd implement that decision professionally — my recommendation doesn't override their authority over the budget and risk tradeoff, that's exactly what the steering committee exists to own.
questions.example: Presentation summary: 'Polling: $12K, 3 weeks, ongoing 5-minute status delay. Event-driven: $28K, 5 weeks, near-real-time status, requires banking partner coordination. Recommendation: event-driven, given payment status visibility affects same-day cash decisions — but this is a budget/risk tradeoff I want the committee's input on.'
commonMistakes: Presenting the decision in technical architecture terms instead of business budget/timeline/risk terms
Using vague claims like 'more robust' without quantifying the concrete cost and benefit
Presenting an unresolved technical debate for the committee to adjudicate rather than a clear recommendation
Not genuinely inviting the committee's input on the risk tradeoff, which is legitimately their decision
Failing to commit to implementing the committee's decision professionally regardless of which option they choose
keyPoints: Translates the technical tradeoff into business terms (budget, timeline, risk)
Quantifies the cost/timeline delta concretely rather than using vague claims
Presents a clear recommendation rather than an unresolved technical debate
Genuinely invites the committee's input on the risk tradeoff as their legitimate decision
Commits to implementing the committee's decision professionally regardless of outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Translates the technical tradeoff into clear business terms
Quantifies cost/timeline/risk concretely rather than vaguely
Presents a clear, defensible recommendation
Appropriately defers final risk/budget judgment to the committee's authority

questions.title: Disagreeing with a Functional Lead's Account Derivation Design
questions.prompt: The functional lead on your project has designed an account derivation rule using a long chain of IF/THEN conditions for a value set that will grow from 8 to 30+ options over the next year — the same mistake you've seen cause maintenance headaches before. The functional lead has more tenure on this account than you. How do you raise your disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer raises the disagreement directly and respectfully rather than either staying silent out of deference to tenure or escalating over the functional lead's head — tenure on the account is not the same as being right about this specific technical design choice, and staying quiet about a known, foreseeable maintenance problem because of seniority dynamics would be a disservice to the client, not genuine respect.

The approach should lead with specific, concrete reasoning rather than a vague 'I don't like this' — referencing the stated growth trajectory (8 to 30+ values) and explaining precisely why mapping sets handle that growth far more maintainably than IF/THEN chains (each addition becomes a mapping set row rather than a rule edit requiring its own testing and change control), and ideally referencing the concrete past experience of this exact pattern causing maintenance headaches, which adds real weight beyond a stylistic preference.

The conversation should be framed collaboratively — raising it as a question or a specific concern to discuss privately first ('I want to flag something about the account rule design before we build further on it — can we talk through the mapping set alternative given where this value set is headed?') rather than publicly undermining the functional lead's design in front of the client or other team members, and should remain genuinely open to being wrong (the functional lead may have a reason for this choice not yet visible) while still being clear and direct about the specific technical concern, rather than softening it into vagueness that doesn't actually get heard or acted on.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd raise this directly, but privately and respectfully — tenure on the account doesn't make someone automatically right about this specific technical choice, and staying quiet about something I genuinely think is going to cause a real maintenance problem isn't actual respect, it's just avoiding an uncomfortable conversation at the client's expense.

I wouldn't lead with a vague 'I'm not sure about this' — I'd be specific. I'd point at the stated growth, 8 values going to 30+ over the next year, and walk through exactly why that favors a mapping set over an IF/THEN chain: every new value becomes a row in a mapping set instead of an edit to the rule itself that needs its own testing and change control. And I'd mention that I've actually seen this specific pattern cause real maintenance headaches before, because that's not just a stylistic opinion, that's a concrete track record.

I'd bring this up privately first, not in front of the client or the wider team — something like, 'before we build further on this account rule, can I flag a concern about the design given where this value set is headed, and walk through an alternative?' And I'd go in genuinely open to being told something I'm not seeing — maybe there's a reason for the IF/THEN approach that isn't obvious to me yet — but I wouldn't soften the actual concern into something vague enough that it doesn't really register. Being direct and being respectful aren't in conflict here; vague is what actually fails both goals.
questions.example: Private conversation: 'Before we build more on top of this account rule — can we talk through using a mapping set instead of the IF/THEN chain, given the value set is going from 8 to 30+? I've seen this exact pattern get really painful to maintain once it scales, and I want to flag it before we're deeper in.'
commonMistakes: Staying silent about the concern out of deference to the functional lead's tenure
Raising the concern vaguely rather than citing the specific growth trajectory and maintenance reasoning
Escalating over the functional lead's head instead of raising it with them directly first
Publicly challenging the design in front of the client or wider team instead of privately
Being so soft/indirect that the actual concern doesn't register or get acted on
keyPoints: Raises the disagreement directly and respectfully rather than staying silent or escalating
Leads with specific, concrete technical reasoning tied to the stated growth trajectory
References concrete past experience with this pattern to add weight
Raises the concern privately and collaboratively rather than publicly
Remains genuinely open to being wrong while staying clear and direct

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Raises the disagreement directly and respectfully rather than avoiding it
Provides specific, concrete technical reasoning for the concern
Handles the conversation privately and collaboratively
Remains genuinely open to being wrong while staying clear

questions.title: Explaining a SQL Reconciliation Finding to Non-Technical Finance Stakeholders
questions.prompt: You ran a SQL-based reconciliation and found a $42,000 discrepancy between AP and the GL, caused by a NULL-handling bug in a report that had been hiding a batch of unaccounted invoices for months. You need to explain this to the controller and CFO, who have no SQL background. How do you present this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer translates the technical root cause into plain business language without either dumbing it down inaccurately or burying the explanation in SQL jargon the audience can't evaluate. The explanation should avoid saying something vague like 'there was a SQL error' (which doesn't actually explain anything to a non-technical audience and sounds alarming without being informative) and instead explain the mechanism in business terms: a report that was supposed to total all unpaid invoices had a flaw that caused it to silently skip invoices missing a specific piece of information, rather than flagging them as missing — so for months, those specific invoices were invisible to the report even though they existed and were unpaid, which is why the $42,000 wasn't previously visible.

The answer should lead with the business impact and the concrete numbers (the $42,000 discrepancy, how many invoices, what period they span) before the technical explanation, since that's what the controller and CFO actually need to act on first, and should be clear about what this does and doesn't mean: these were real, legitimate unpaid invoices that simply weren't being counted, not fraud, not double-counting, and not a current cash shortfall beyond what these invoices already represented — being precise about what the finding does and doesn't imply matters a great deal when presenting a financial discrepancy to executives.

The answer should close with the remediation: the report itself has been corrected (explaining briefly, in plain terms, what was fixed — the report now explicitly flags incomplete records instead of silently dropping them), the $42,000 in invoices have been identified and are being processed through normal AP workflow, and a broader check should be offered to see if the same flaw affected any other reports that share similar logic, which is the kind of proactive follow-through that actually earns confidence after a finding like this.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd lead with the business impact first, not the technical cause — '$42,000 in legitimate unpaid invoices from the last several months were sitting in the system but weren't showing up on the report we use to total unpaid AP. We found them, and here's what we're doing about it.' That's what they actually need to hear first.

Then I'd explain the mechanism in plain language, not SQL terms. I wouldn't say 'there was a SQL bug,' because that's technically true but tells them nothing useful and just sounds alarming. I'd say something like: 'the report that totals unpaid invoices had a flaw where, if an invoice was missing one specific piece of information, the report would just silently skip it entirely instead of flagging it as incomplete — so these invoices existed and were genuinely unpaid, they just weren't being counted by that particular report for months.'

And I'd be really precise about what this does and doesn't mean, because that distinction matters a lot to a CFO hearing a $42,000 number — this is not fraud, it's not double-counted, and it's not some new cash shortfall beyond what these invoices already represented on their own; it's invoices that were real the whole time and just weren't visible in this one report.

Then I'd close with what's being done: the report's been fixed so it flags incomplete records instead of silently dropping them, the $42,000 in invoices are identified and moving through normal AP processing now, and I'd proactively offer to check whether any other reports share that same underlying logic flaw — because that's the kind of follow-through that actually rebuilds confidence after finding something like this, not just fixing the one instance.
questions.example: Executive summary: '$42,000 in real, unpaid invoices from the last four months weren't showing on our unpaid-AP report because of a flaw that silently skipped invoices missing one specific field instead of flagging them. Not fraud, not double-counted — just invisible to that one report. Fixed, invoices now in normal AP processing, and I'm checking other reports for the same flaw.'
commonMistakes: Using technical jargon ('NULL handling,' 'SQL bug') without translating it into plain business language
Leading with the technical cause instead of the business impact and concrete numbers
Not being precise about what the finding does and doesn't imply (not fraud, not a new shortfall)
Omitting the remediation plan and proactive check for similar issues in other reports
Presenting the finding in a way that sounds alarming without being informative
keyPoints: Translates the technical root cause into plain, accurate business language
Leads with business impact and concrete numbers before the technical explanation
Is precise about what the finding does and doesn't mean (no fraud, no new shortfall)
Presents a clear remediation plan for both the invoices and the underlying report flaw
Proactively offers to check for the same issue elsewhere to build confidence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Translates the technical cause accurately into plain business language
Leads with business impact and concrete numbers appropriately
Is precise about what the finding does and doesn't imply
Presents a clear remediation plan including proactive follow-through

questions.title: Managing Conflicting Priorities During Period-End Close
questions.prompt: During a tight period-end close, you're simultaneously asked by the controller to investigate an urgent subledger reconciliation variance, by a project manager to finish configuration testing for an unrelated go-live next week, and by a junior colleague who's stuck and needs help — all three say their request is the priority. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer resists simply trying to satisfy all three requesters simultaneously (which usually means doing all three poorly) and instead makes a deliberate, communicated prioritization decision, recognizing that 'everyone says their thing is the priority' is a common situation that requires someone to actually rank the requests against real business consequence rather than against who asked most recently or most forcefully.

The reasoning should weigh actual business impact and reversibility: a period-end close reconciliation variance has a hard deadline (the close itself) and blocks other people's work until resolved, typically making it the highest-priority item; the go-live configuration testing has a deadline next week, which is real but has more slack than the close happening now; and the junior colleague being stuck has real cost (their time, and a growing problem if left unresolved) but may be addressable with a shorter intervention (a quick unblocking conversation) rather than requiring sustained attention.

The answer should describe communicating this prioritization transparently to all three rather than silently deciding and leaving people guessing — telling the controller their variance is the immediate priority, telling the project manager realistically when the configuration testing will actually get attention given the close, and giving the junior colleague a short, bounded unblock (a focused 15-minute conversation to get them moving again, rather than either ignoring them or dropping everything for them) — managing expectations explicitly is itself the actual skill being tested here, not just picking correctly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't try to actually do all three at once — that usually means doing all three badly. Someone has to actually rank these against real business consequence, not against who asked loudest or most recently, and that's on me here, not something I can dodge.

The close reconciliation variance has a hard deadline — the close itself — and it's blocking other people's work until it's resolved, so that's the highest priority, full stop. The go-live configuration testing has a real deadline too, but it's next week, which gives it more slack than something that's blocking the close happening right now. And my junior colleague being stuck has a real cost — their time, and a problem that gets worse the longer it sits — but that one's probably solvable with a short, focused intervention rather than needing my sustained attention for hours.

So what I'd actually do: tell the controller their variance is my immediate focus right now. Tell the project manager honestly when the configuration testing is realistically going to get real attention given the close — not vaguely, an actual time estimate. And give my junior colleague a bounded fifteen-minute conversation to get them unstuck and moving again, rather than either brushing them off completely or dropping the close work to sit with them for two hours. The actual skill here isn't magically picking the one 'correct' priority — it's making the ranking and then being transparent about it with all three people, instead of silently deciding and leaving everyone guessing where they stand.
questions.example: Communicated plan: 'Controller — I'm on the variance now, that's my top priority.' 'PM — I can't start config testing until this afternoon given the close; realistically you'll have my full attention on it by 2pm.' 'Junior colleague — give me 15 minutes right now, let's get you unstuck, then I need to get back to the close issue.'
commonMistakes: Trying to work on all three requests simultaneously instead of making a deliberate priority decision
Prioritizing based on who asked most recently or most forcefully rather than actual business impact
Silently deciding a priority order without communicating it to the other two requesters
Either completely ignoring the junior colleague or dropping everything else to help them at length
Not giving the project manager a realistic, specific timeline instead of a vague deferral
keyPoints: Makes a deliberate prioritization decision rather than attempting all three at once
Weighs actual business impact, deadline hardness, and reversibility in the ranking
Communicates the prioritization transparently to all three stakeholders
Provides a bounded, appropriately-scoped intervention for the junior colleague
Gives the deferred stakeholder (PM) a realistic, specific timeline rather than a vague answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Makes a sound, reasoned prioritization decision across the three requests
Weighs business impact and deadline hardness accurately
Communicates the decision transparently to all three stakeholders
Provides an appropriately-scoped response to the junior colleague

questions.title: Pushing Back on Scope Creep in an Order-to-Cash Customization Request
questions.prompt: Midway through configuring standard Order-to-Cash functionality, the client's sales operations manager asks you to build a custom pricing override screen that falls well outside the agreed project scope, saying 'it's just a small add-on, our last consultant would have just done it.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer doesn't simply refuse outright (which risks the relationship and ignores that there may be a legitimate underlying business need) or simply absorb the work to avoid conflict (which sets a precedent that erodes scope discipline for the rest of the project and is unfair to the project's budget and timeline commitments). The response should first genuinely assess whether 'small add-on' is accurate — a custom pricing override screen is very unlikely to be small; it typically involves new UI/extension development, validation logic, security considerations for who can override pricing and under what approval, and testing, which is a different category of work from configuring standard functionality already in scope.

The answer should address the 'our last consultant would have just done it' comment directly but professionally — without criticizing the prior consultant specifically, explaining that scope exists to protect the project's budget and timeline commitments that were agreed with the client's own leadership, and that absorbing unscoped work silently would be a disservice to those commitments, not a favor; this reframes the conversation away from 'will you do me a favor' to 'how do we handle a real need responsibly.'

The resolution should offer a clear path rather than a flat no: documenting this as a change request with its own estimate for scope, cost, and timeline impact, to be approved through whatever change control process governs the project, and in the meantime asking what need is actually driving this request — there may be a way to meet the underlying business need using existing, in-scope functionality (e.g., existing approval/hold mechanisms) that the sales operations manager isn't aware of, which could resolve the need without any scope change at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't just say an outright no, and I wouldn't just quietly build it either — both of those are bad options for different reasons. Refusing flat out risks the relationship and ignores that there might be a real business need behind this. But absorbing it silently sets a precedent that scope just doesn't mean anything on this project anymore, and that's not fair to the budget and timeline commitments that were actually agreed to.

First, I'd actually check whether 'small add-on' is even accurate, because a custom pricing override screen almost never is — that's new UI development, validation logic, security considerations around who's allowed to override pricing and under what approval, and its own testing. That's a genuinely different category of work from configuring standard functionality that's already in scope.

On the 'our last consultant would have just done it' comment — I wouldn't take a shot at the previous consultant, but I would reframe it: scope exists to protect the budget and timeline commitments that were agreed to with their own leadership, and quietly absorbing unscoped work isn't actually doing them a favor, it's putting those commitments at risk without anyone having agreed to that tradeoff.

What I'd actually offer is a real path forward, not a wall: I'd document this as a change request with its own estimate for scope, cost, and timeline, run through whatever change control process governs this project. And in the meantime, I'd genuinely ask what's actually driving the request — there's a real chance the underlying business need can be met with something already in scope, like existing approval or hold mechanisms, that the sales ops manager just doesn't know is already available. That could solve this with zero scope change at all.
questions.example: Response: 'A custom pricing override screen is more than a small add-on — new UI, validation, approval security, testing. Let's document this as a change request with its own estimate so it goes through proper approval. In the meantime, can you tell me what's actually driving this need? There may be a way to handle it with the approval/hold functionality already in scope.'
commonMistakes: Refusing the request outright without exploring the underlying business need
Silently absorbing the unscoped work to avoid conflict, setting a bad precedent
Accepting the 'small add-on' framing without assessing the real scope impact
Criticizing the previous consultant rather than reframing the conversation around scope's purpose
Not offering a constructive path forward (change request process, alternative existing functionality)
keyPoints: Avoids both outright refusal and silent absorption of unscoped work
Accurately assesses the real scope impact rather than accepting the 'small' framing
Reframes the 'last consultant' comment professionally around scope's purpose
Offers a clear change-request path rather than a flat no
Proactively explores whether existing in-scope functionality could meet the real need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both outright refusal and silent scope absorption
Accurately assesses the real scope/effort impact of the request
Handles the 'last consultant' comment professionally and constructively
Offers a constructive path forward (change request, alternative solution)

questions.title: Handling a Missed Deadline on an AP Invoice Automation Deliverable
questions.prompt: You committed to delivering an automated FBDI-based invoice loading process by Friday, but discovered on Thursday that a dependency (a supplier data cleanup owned by another team) wasn't actually finished, making your Friday deadline impossible. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer communicates the risk to the deadline as soon as it's discovered (Thursday), rather than waiting until Friday to announce a miss, which gives stakeholders the maximum possible time to adjust plans, re-sequence other work, or help unblock the dependency — silence until the deadline itself is the most damaging version of this situation, since it removes everyone else's ability to react.

The communication should be specific and accountable without either over-apologizing in a way that centers the consultant's feelings over the problem, or deflecting entirely onto the other team as if the consultant bears no responsibility for not having caught this dependency risk earlier. A balanced answer acknowledges that the dependency should ideally have been tracked and flagged earlier in the project (a lesson for next time) while being factual that the supplier data cleanup is owned by the other team and is the actual blocker — both things can be true: the consultant should have surfaced this risk sooner, and the other team's incomplete work is the direct cause of the miss.

The answer should propose a concrete path forward rather than just reporting the problem: a realistic new timeline based on when the dependency is actually expected to complete (checked directly with the other team, not guessed), and ideally a partial or interim deliverable if one is possible (e.g., completing and testing everything in the load process that doesn't depend on the cleaned supplier data, so not all progress is blocked) — demonstrating that the response to a missed deadline is to minimize further damage and keep moving, not just to explain why it happened.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd flag this the moment I found out on Thursday, not wait until Friday to announce a miss — that's the single most important part of handling this well. Finding out Thursday and staying quiet until the deadline actually arrives takes away everyone else's ability to react, re-sequence their own work, or help get the dependency unblocked. Silence until the last minute is the worst version of this.

When I raise it, I'd be specific and accountable without either over-apologizing or shifting all the blame onto the other team. Honestly, both things are true here — I probably should have been tracking and flagging this dependency risk earlier in the project instead of discovering it on Thursday, and that's a real lesson for next time. At the same time, the supplier data cleanup is genuinely owned by the other team, and their incomplete work is the direct, factual cause of the miss. I'd say both of those plainly instead of picking one and hiding the other.

Then I wouldn't just report the problem and stop there — I'd bring a path forward. I'd check directly with the other team on a realistic completion date for the cleanup, not guess at one, and give a new timeline based on that actual answer. And I'd see if there's a partial deliverable I can still get done now — finishing and testing everything in the load process that doesn't actually depend on the cleaned supplier data, so the whole thing isn't sitting dead in the water waiting on someone else's work.
questions.example: Thursday message: 'Flagging now, not waiting for tomorrow — the supplier data cleanup this load depends on isn't finished, so I can't hit Friday. I should have flagged this dependency risk earlier, and I'll own that. I've confirmed with [other team] they expect it done Tuesday; I'll target Wednesday for the full load. In the meantime, I'm finishing and testing the parts of the load process that don't depend on the cleaned data.'
commonMistakes: Waiting until the Friday deadline to announce the miss instead of flagging it Thursday
Deflecting all responsibility onto the other team without acknowledging the dependency should have been tracked earlier
Over-apologizing in a way that centers feelings over the actual problem and path forward
Guessing at a new timeline instead of checking directly with the other team
Not identifying any partial/interim progress that could still be made despite the blocker
keyPoints: Communicates the risk as soon as discovered, not at the deadline itself
Balances genuine accountability with factual acknowledgment of the actual blocker
Checks directly with the other team for a realistic new timeline rather than guessing
Identifies a partial/interim deliverable to keep progress moving despite the blocker
Avoids both over-apologizing and complete deflection of responsibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Communicates the risk promptly upon discovery rather than at the deadline
Balances genuine accountability with factual acknowledgment of the real blocker
Proposes a realistic new timeline based on direct confirmation
Identifies a partial/interim deliverable to minimize further delay

questions.title: Handing Off Subledger Accounting Configuration Knowledge at the End of an Engagement
questions.prompt: Your consulting engagement is ending in two weeks, and you're the only person who really understands the custom account derivation rules and mapping sets you built for the client's Subledger Accounting setup. The client's internal team is competent but wasn't deeply involved in the build. How do you approach the knowledge handoff?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats knowledge handoff as a planned deliverable with its own scope and timeline, not an informal afterthought squeezed into the last few days — two weeks is enough time to do this well only if it's structured deliberately from day one of those two weeks, rather than left until the final days when there's no longer room to address gaps that surface.

The answer should describe layered documentation that serves different future needs: a design rationale document explaining why each non-obvious account rule or mapping set was built the way it was (not just what it does, which can often be read directly from the configuration, but why — what business requirement or edge case drove this specific design choice), since the 'why' is what's actually lost when the builder leaves and is hardest to reconstruct later; and a practical troubleshooting guide covering the specific failure modes the consultant has already seen during the build (e.g., 'if invoices in category X fail to derive a complete account, check mapping set Y first, this has happened before for reason Z').

The answer should also include active knowledge transfer, not just written documentation: walking the client's internal team through live scenarios together (e.g., together adding a new value to a mapping set, or together diagnosing a deliberately-introduced test failure) so they've actually exercised the skill before the consultant leaves, not just read about it — and should include an honest assessment of remaining risk, flagging specific areas where two weeks genuinely isn't enough for the internal team to reach full independent competence, so the client can plan for that (extended support, a follow-up engagement) rather than being surprised by a gap after the consultant is already gone.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this as a real deliverable with its own plan, not something I scramble to throw together in the last couple of days — two weeks is actually enough time to do this properly, but only if I structure it from day one of those two weeks rather than leaving it for the end when there's no room left to fix gaps I find.

I'd build two layers of documentation. First, a design rationale document — not just what each account rule and mapping set does, because honestly a lot of that can be read directly out of the configuration itself, but why I built it that way. What business requirement or edge case actually drove this specific design? That's the part that's genuinely lost the moment I walk out the door, and it's the hardest thing to reconstruct later without me. Second, a practical troubleshooting guide based on actual failure modes I've already hit during the build — 'if invoices in this category fail to derive a complete account, check this mapping set first, here's why this has happened before.'

But I wouldn't stop at documents — I'd do active transfer too. I'd sit with their internal team and actually walk through live scenarios together, like adding a new value to a mapping set together, or diagnosing a test failure I deliberately introduce, so they've actually done it with me there before I'm gone, not just read about how to do it.

And I'd be honest about where the real risk still is. If there are specific areas where I genuinely don't think two weeks gets their team to full independent competence, I'd say so directly, so the client can plan for that — extended support, a short follow-up engagement — instead of being blindsided by a gap after I've already left.
questions.example: Week 1: design rationale doc for all custom account rules/mapping sets, written and reviewed with the internal team. Week 2: live joint sessions — adding a mapping set value together, diagnosing a deliberately broken test case together — plus an honest risk note flagging that the multi-representation rules for the secondary ledger will likely need follow-up support beyond the two weeks.
commonMistakes: Leaving knowledge transfer as an informal afterthought squeezed into the final days
Documenting only what the configuration does rather than why it was built that way
Relying solely on written documentation without active, hands-on joint exercises
Not being honest about areas where two weeks is genuinely insufficient for full competence
Not giving the client time to plan for remaining risk (extended support, follow-up engagement)
keyPoints: Treats knowledge handoff as a planned deliverable structured from day one of the remaining time
Documents design rationale (why), not just configuration behavior (what)
Includes a practical troubleshooting guide based on real observed failure modes
Includes active, hands-on joint exercises, not just written documentation
Honestly flags remaining risk areas so the client can plan for them proactively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Structures the handoff as a deliberate, planned deliverable across the full remaining time
Documents design rationale and practical troubleshooting, not just configuration behavior
Includes active, hands-on knowledge transfer, not only written documentation
Honestly assesses and communicates remaining risk areas
